### Reviewer 3

Review of Hayden et al.
This is a very well written paper on changing Aurora subglacial drainage at different climate states that is based on a
finite-element glacier drainage system model which responds to climate forcing through a link between ice thickness and
water pressure at the bed. Using this methodology forced today with BedMachine for the topography and ISMIP6 for the
climate they simulate potential drainage pattern under Totten which seems reasonable.
They then attempt similar situations at the Eocene-Oligocene boundary and at the mid-Miocene. For the latter I think they are
seeking to simulate the Mid-Miocene Climatic Optimum. There are issues with specifically matching the O-18 curve with
CO2 as the authors are undoubtedly aware, but I don’t think this matters for the paper since you are forcing it at two CO2
states roughly equivalent to E-O and MMCO. The specific date does not matter for your study since as noted below, I don’t
think you are yet able to simulate what specifically occurred with the ice sheet and drainage system at the E-O and MMCO.
The larger issues however are three:
1) bed topography has certainly evolved from the Eocene to today and thus what is the sensitivity of the model to this
process since we do not have a E-O or Mid-Mio bedmachine? There are some sentences discussing how it might have
changed but I was left unclear as the expected magnitude and feedbacks if say the deeper basins under ASB we not yet
filled in and we had a subglacier lake scenario, or if the erosion through time has substantially changed the overall gradient
to flatter today than in the E-O run. Can we be confident of these glacial drainage change results in absence of the
topography? Some sensitivity study/discussion is needed to place these results in context on this issue.
2) The ice margin for the ASB portion of East Antarctica is not substantially changing between the E-O, Mid-Mio, Today, and
Future scenarios. There is certainly some retreat and some advance aspects but these are way too small to match the
offshore shelf and slope geophysical data implying presence or absence of grounded ice (Gulick et al., 2017, Nature,
Montelli et al. 2019 GSA Bulletin, McKay et al., 2022, Ant Clim Evol). For instance, at the E-O boundary there were tunnel
valleys > 125 km seaward of the current ice margin which require grounded ice and we have a glacial shelf crossing trough
(Donda et al., 2020, Ant Sci; Hirano et al., 2023, Nature Comm) reaching the shelf edge during the advances. There is strong
data for grounded ice therefore over much of the shelf and within the trough to the shelf edge since there is a large trough
mouth fan for the Totten system active in the Oligocene at least. Therefore your E-O simulation ice margin should be
substantially more advanced to match this geologic evidence. In counterpoint, there appears to have been no evidence of
proximal glacial sedimentary products in the MMCO on the shelf and thus one would infer a much more retreated ice margin
to explain this. Your Mid-Mio simulation is somewhat retreated but probably far too little to explain the absence of glacial
sedimentary facies at the MMCO on the shelf.
3) The lack of greater changes in ice margin at warmer and colder periods imply the current models are missing some key
feedbacks. It could be the effect of ice cliff instability as raised by the authors. However another key change that should
occur is going from colder to warmer based glaciers such as is seen in north versus south Greenland outlet glaciers where
warmer wetter ones moving larger volumes of sediment potentially building glacial moraines or morainal banks, and are
correlated with tunnel valleys existing when advancing onto shelves (e.g., Alaska, North Sea). Colder states act more like
modern Antarctica or the colder based parts of Greenland forming grounding zone wedges instead and substantially less
feedbacks are likely. As Totten system transitioned to this more polar state only the Late Miocene-Pliocene, it is probably
incorrect to assume the subglacial system worked the same way from a more modern polar state as it did in a past more
dynamic state. In other words E-O and Mid-Mio likely dynamically behaved more like the North Sea or Alaska systems than
Pleistocene Antarctica in order to explain the greatly different shelf margin effects and glacial sedimentary products. What
exactly is the change in feedbacks is that allows for much more dynamic advance and retreat cycles is not yet known of
course but some combination of melt water, warm bases, and glacial sediment dynamics are likely involved.
Moving forward with this paper I think the authors need to specifically note how the paleo model runs do not produce
dynamic enough advances to reach the shelf edge during the E-O or leave the shelf entirely ice free during the Mid-Miocene
and then discuss the possible additional feedbacks needed to result in greater ice margin changes. Then discuss what effect
this would have on the subglacial networks that are the focus of this paper. In summary, this paper does a good job with
the paleo models if the bed topography did not differ substantially and if the glacial dynamics did not change going into past
climate states. Issue is we know the ice was a lot further advanced and have evidence of a wetter more dynamic system that
created tunnel valleys, trough mouth fans, and probably intermittent morainal banks … how is this kind of system, one more
representative of the LGM Alaska, North Sea, or West Greenland for instance, differ from what is modeled in this paper?
Given there is clearly a mismatch in ice edge position with the geologic record at least for maximum advance and retreat
climate states, then how can we use this paper’s results to inform us of process without yet being able to include all the
processes required? I think the path forward is to use the paleo model results to discuss how different inputs such as CO2
affect ice thickness and water pressure and drainage without making the argument that this study is faithfully
reproducing the conditions at E-O and Mid-Mio. Consider what you models are not including and how you might then frame your model
results differently since its interesting the tradeoffs observed in water pressure and drainage length in your work, and
considering future scenarios (see below), but these models clearly do not represent the state of the ASB glacial system at
the E-O or mid-Mio.
For the future model runs, I think these are fine and in fact really interesting suggestions for future
states, if the system stays in its current polar mode of dynamics. However, if it switches modes to the way it operated in the
Oligocene to Miocene then there would be expected a much greater dynamic change possibility that could be acknowledged.
On the writing, this paper is remarkably free of typos, has excellently written sentences, and was very clear to read. Only
minor item on that front is that the word further (a concept) is used in two places where the word should be farther (a
distance).
My recommendation is therefore Major Revisions to consider the issues with mismatch to the geologic record and
suggestions of glacial dynamics having a warmer wetter regime with processes not yet included in the finite glacial drainage
system modeling.
Hopefully this review will be helpful and I would be willing to do a re-review as needed,
Sean Gulick

## Authors' Response to Round 1

Reply to reviewers
The past, present, and future evolution of Aurora Subglacial Basin’s subglacial drainage system
Hayden, Pelle, and Dow
We would like to thank the reviewers for their comments. We have addressed the comments point-
for-point below. The comments are laid out in normal font, and our replies are in italic green font.
Reviewer 1:
This paper uses a subglacial hydrology model to understand how the subglacial drainage system
of the Aurora Subglacial Basin in East Antarctica would respond either in the past or in the future
to changes in ice sheet configuration. A series of warm time periods from the past are tested using
input data from topographic reconstructions or modern topography and from a set of ice sheet
models that have been used to understand warm-period response in this region. The model predicts
where and how much subglacial discharge occurs, how it is routed to the edge of the continent and
thereafter, using a plume model, how that water would translate into melt rates beneath the ice
shelf. The outcomes of each model show quite significant differences in subglacial water flow
pattern and rate, as well as differences in how the water reaches the margin (e.g. through a trunk
vs. multiple outlets) which therefore has a knock-on impact on the pattern of melting under the ice
shelf. A key point is that under retreated ice scenarios, the drainage system tends to become longer
and produces more water, delivering that to the grounding line where it could enhance ice shelf
melting significantly. It is also useful that the authors highlight that its not as simple as using a
paleo warm-period scenario as an analogue for future warming impacts. The work does, as the
authors say, represent the first time the hydraulic system has been investigated for this range of ice
sheet change scenarios and in that respect the key results are impactful. Indeed, it is an interesting
paper and the quality of the work is excellent. The work is largely valid in terms of predicting
subglacial hydraulic changes, but as you can see with my two comments below, there are places
where some additional consideration would help the manuscript. The approach and data are
appropriate, although there are also questions relating to some sensitivity tests (second comment
below).
Suggested Improvements:
However, my first significant concern around the work is that it is not as impactful as it could be
because the points about the impact on ice velocity and buttressing which are used at the end of
the paper to outline why this work is impactful are not actually tested. In other words, outputs of
basal water conditions or ice shelf basal melting are not subsequently fed back into ice sheet
models in any way to demonstrate/quantify the importance. Thus although we can hypothesise that
the impacts on ice behaviour and mass change would be significant, this isn’t directly shown. I
realise you signal that next steps would be to couple things together in an ice sheet model, but
there is a half-way house (via perturbation experiments) which would hammer home the
significance of this work. Thus the impact of the changing hydrologic regime on the ice sheet feels
somewhat speculative at present because the impact on the ice sheet is not fully tested. If it could
be firmed up in some way it would really demonstrate the significance of the results more clearly
as well as becoming of interest to a broader readership.
Thank you for raising this important point and for your help in maximising the impact of our
results. During the time this manuscript was in review, coauthor Pelle and colleagues published
complementary work that presents future 2100 projections of the Aurora Subglacial Basin in a
coupled ice-subglacial hydrology model (ISSM-GlaDS) to test the sensitivity of outlet glacier
behaviour to future subglacial and ocean forcing (Pelle et al., 2024). In their projections, they
found that ice-subglacial water feedbacks (ice shelf melt enhancements and increased grounded
ice basal sliding) increased the ASB sea level contribution by 30%, drove earlier onset of retreat
of Totten’s southern grounding zone by ~25 years, and led to continual accelerated retreat of
Vanderford and Adams Glaciers over the full 83-year projection. These new results confirm our
hypothesis of the strong impact that subglacial processes can have on outlet glacier dynamics.
Thus, in the revised manuscript, we have framed our results in the context of these new findings
(L360-370):
“We note that in a complementary study, Pelle et al.24 developed a coupled ISSM-GlaDS
configuration of ASB and, in projections to 2100, found that subglacial discharge-driven melt
enhancements led to earlier onset of retreat of Totten Glacier’s southern grounding zone by ~25
years and continually accelerated retreat of Vanderford Glacier (up to 10 km of additional retreat
compared to uncoupled “ISSM-only” simulations). That is, while the magnitude of these discharge
melt enhancements is small relative to the background ocean-driven melt signal, their location at
deep grounding line points has cascading impacts on the upstream stress regime of entire glacial
basins. As such, the highly sensitive nature of the melt enhancements presented here highlights the
importance of better constraining subglacial hydrology model inputs and boundary conditions,
which will, in turn, improve simulations of past, present, and future ice sheet dynamics.”
We note that Pelle et al. only ran two subglacial scenarios (a low and high emission climate
forcing) due to the computational cost of running the coupled models through 2100 and thus did
not test the sensitivity of the system to variations in subglacial water input and changes in ice/bed
geometry as we have explored in our manuscript. They also did not perform paleo-simulations.
Nonetheless, we argue that the significance of our work is that we simulate paleo, modern, and
future ASB subglacial hydrology in a consistent modelling framework and can highlight model
sensitivity to the various inputs.

disagreement and compare model results with what we know about subglacial hydrology in the
region from the geologic record.
Concerning the choice of the Mid-Miocene grounding line location, we are unable to comment as
the grounding line configurations are from the Paxman et al. (2020) data. However, the reviewer
raises an excellent point, that it is important to compare the model outputs to the geologic record.
Therefore, we have now expanded on this in the discussion (L414-451, see response to above
comment) and supplementary material (Text S3; L181-212, see response to above comment).
Past sea level: there is substantial data to suggest significant changes in sea level in the past. Was
past sea level considered in the modeling exercise? How might past sea level impact the choice of
grounding line locations in the paleo model runs? We do know that sea level dropped to -30 to -
40 m relative to modern day across the EO boundary (Miller et al., 2020), which likely enabled
grounded ice expansion from the ASB across the continental shelf, as observed in the geologic
record. Further, during the Miocene Climate Optimum (~16 Ma), sea levels may have been +50m
higher than present (likely overestimate), while at ~14 Ma, sea levels may have been -40 m lower
than present. This is another reason why the authors really need to clarify if they are talking about
the MCO (~16 Ma) or ice expansion and stabilization associated with the Middle Miocene Climate
Transition at ~14 Ma.
Our subglacial hydrology model is run over grounded ice only, with the grounding line locations
and ice geometries extracted from Paxman et al. (2020); we have now clarified this in the main
text and methods. As the grounding lines are determined by the ice thickness relative to sea level
the Paxman et al. (2020) data are our only control for sea level. Accounting for sea level changes
would require specialised ice sheet-sea level modelling experiments, which are beyond the scope
of our study. We have also endeavoured to clarify in the main text that we are modelling the
subglacial hydrology at the Middle Miocene Climate Transition, as this is the time snapshot from
Paxman et al.’s (2020) data (see L124-127 and response to above comment):
“Our paleo subglacial hydrology simulations use grounding lines, ice sheet geometries, and basal
inputs from Paxman et al.26. We focus on the Eocene-Oligocene Boundary (34 Mya) and the Mid-
Miocene Climate Transition (14 Mya; hereafter Mid-Miocene) as these intervals correspond to
ice volumes in ASB that are larger and smaller, respectively, than those in the present day26.”
Paleo channel locations: there are paleo channel systems identified both in the subglacial
landscapes (see Young et al., 2011, Aitken et al., 2016) inland of Ridge A and on the continental
shelf seaward of the current study’s boundaries (see Gulick, Shevenell et al., 2017; Fernandez et
al., 2018; Montelli et al., 2020). How do the model results compare with the locations of these
channels? Some discussion of the modelled channel locations vs observed channel locations would
strengthen the discussion of model results and the impact of the manuscript.
This is an excellent suggestion, and we agree that comparing our model results to observations
would strengthen the paper. Unfortunately, the data from the publications indicated above by the
reviewer are either not publicly available, or in a format that we are unable to use. For instance,
the plotted data in Gulick et al.’s paper are from thousands of survey lines, the precise locations
of the inferred tunnel valleys are not provided, and the depths are provided as two-way travel
times. Converting the data into a usable form requires specialist knowledge of MB-System seafloor
mapping software, which is outside the scope of our paper. Also, we approximated the tunnel
valley locations from Gulick et al.’s Figure 1b, line 21, and found that the inferred locations were
outside of our model domain. However, in the supplementary material of our revised submission,
we have commented on the location of tunnel valleys and our modelled channel locations and the
possible reasons for the mismatch (see Text S3).
MICI as a viable mass loss mechanism: the authors admit the tenuous nature of the MICI mechanism in ice sheet models.
This reviewer is of the opinion that inclusion of MICI in the runs and in any discussion diminishes the results, as presented
(mostly because the reader is left being skeptical of MICI, rather than thinking about the present modelling study). Would it
be better to think about and address how substantial subglacial meltwater presence might eliminate the need for a MICI-type
mechanism to generate a responsive ice sheet? Such an argument, if possible, would really highlight the need to
understand subglacial hydrologic systems, past and present.
The reviewer has raised concerns about our discussion of MICI, indicating that it detracts from
the impact of our results. We agree that, in our paper, we could have been clearer about the
rationale for discussing MICI. In the revised paper’s introduction and final paragraph, while we
have kept the comparison of MICI and non-MICI results, we have now more explicitly mentioned
the implications of subglacial hydrology for initiating large-scale ice sheet changes without
requiring MICI. This is a key argument for incorporating the role of hydrology in ice sheet
dynamic analysis and, therefore, we believe retaining the MICI experiments is a valuable output
for the community:
L70-72 “Still, since most ice sheet models neglect evolving subglacial hydrology, it has seldom
been considered that changes to subglacial drainage systems may be sufficient to initiate large-
scale ice dynamic and geometric changes without the need for MICI.”
L459-464 “Although our hydrology model was not coupled to ice and ocean models, our results
allow us to shed light on the effects of large-scale drainage reorganisation and the consequences
of neglecting evolving subglacial hydrology in ice sheet models. If high water pressure were to
move upglacier and higher grounding line channel discharges were to weaken ice shelf
buttressing, subglacial water alone could drive sea level contributions from Antarctica that are
larger than previously suggested, without the need for instability mechanisms such as MICI.”
Generally, after reading this manuscript, it seems that the authors have missed an opportunity to
compare model runs with existing observations of subglacial hydrologic systems in this catchment.
This is one of the only locations in Antarctica where such a comparison is possible. Such an
exercise would significantly strengthen the believability and impact of the modeling studies. I
recommend such a data-model comparison be undertaken before publication is considered.
We agree that the manuscript is significantly strengthened with a comparison of model outputs to
observations and thus we have now added this to the revised manuscript (L414-451; see above
response) and the supplementary material (Text S3; see above response).
A few more minor questions/comments on the manuscript, in no particular order:
This study currently uses outdated CO2 reconstructions. I recommend using the latest CO2
compilation (CENCO2PIP Consortium, 2023).
Unfortunately, since we are using reconstructions from Paxman et al. (2020), we are unable to
use alternative CO2 compilations. We hope this is now clearer in the text.
Figure 1 and its caption are quite confusing (there might be a typo for the E-O simulation- should
it be C and H panels?). It would be helpful to list the time intervals above the model domains and
basal input as in Figure 4, and maybe place vertical lines between the time intervals.
Reviewer 1 raised a similar point about Figure 1, and we have thus updated this figure.
Why does the Law Dome region disappear in the Mid-Miocene simulation? Is this related to sea
level? And, if it is, the same would be true for the Eocene, would it not?
We thank the reviewer for raising this point. The domains for all simulations were calculated based
on hydraulic potential analysis using the ice and bed geometry from the source publication (in the
paleo runs, these data were from Paxman et al. (2020). Because of this flow routing, Law Dome
lies outside our calculated domain in the Mid-Miocene simulation, but within the domain for the
Eocene-Oligocene Boundary simulation. We have clarified this in the methods (L504-505):
“Since hydraulic potential analysis is based on the geometry of the ice and bed, the source data
in this calculation influence the flow routing and, therefore, the domain size.”
I don't understand the discussion of ice shelves in past ice configurations. There is no evidence of
ice shelf presence in the Eocene or the middle Miocene, but rather grounded ice on the continental
shelves. How does this fact impact the results of this study?
We apologise for causing confusion about the scope of our work and the influence of ice shelves.
We need to be clear that the goal of our study was not to model hydrology and ice shelf interactions
exactly as they were and will be, nor to validate the exact configuration of ice during these time
periods, although Paxman et al. 2020 paleo topographies were constrained by independent
geological data. Rather, our aim was to show how the feedbacks between subglacial hydrology
and ice shelves could influence the entire glacier system, and the importance of including these
interactions within a coupled ice sheet model, hydrology, and ice shelf framework. We were not
sufficiently clear on this aim in the original manuscript, and we have endeavoured to make this
clear in the revised version by amending the text in the introduction (L128-131):
“The purpose of these experiments is to provide a large-scale overview of how changes in ice
configurations and basal (melt, velocity, and topography) conditions influence ASB’s subglacial
drainage system and are not intended to be interpreted as the exact subglacial conditions during
each of these paleo time snapshots.”
Fernandez et al (2018) present pretty interesting data for meltwater input to the shelf region during
the last deglaciation (see bedrock channels and stacked grounding zone wedges termed feather
moraines in the publication). Would this be a useful time interval over which to test the model,
considering that we have knowledge about the location of the ice sheet and of subglacial meltwater
output/presence during the last deglaciation just based on continental shelf geomorphology.
We agree that this would be an interesting time snapshot to investigate. The Paxman et al. (2020)
study did not perform simulations at the last deglaciation, and, therefore, we do not have ice sheet
model data that will allow us to investigate the hydrology during this time period.
What happens if surface-derived meltwater is included for the MCO run?
We were intrigued by this suggestion, and thus, we have investigated the distribution of surface
meltwater during the Mid-Miocene run. We ran a Mid-Miocene simulation where the surface
meltwater produced by Paxman et al.’s (2020) ice sheet modelling experiments was added directly
to the bed. These additional meltwater inputs are spatially-variable, but temporally constant (i.e.,
not seasonally varying) and applied over the entire transient simulation of 10 000 days. Since this
additional melt is temporally fixed, there is no seasonal expansion and contraction of channels
that would accommodate time-varying volumes of meltwater, resulting in temporally varying
channel discharges. Therefore, this test likely represents the upper bound of the influence of
surface melt on basal hydrology. We adopt this simplified approach due to the uncertainties in the
timing, locations, and volumes of surface meltwater in the paleo record. We found that adding
surface meltwater increases the total discharge in channels but does not change the locations of
channels since the surface melt is concentrated near the grounding line, where channels have
already formed:
[figure redacted]
Based on this investigation, in the discussion, we have added a comment on the influence that
adding surface melt has on the drainage system and noted it as a future research priority (L417-
430):
“However, constraining the timing, volume, and location of meltwater inputs to the bed remains
challenging due to the inherent uncertainties in interpreting the time-integrated paleo record, and
these uncertainties translate to difficulties in determining the most appropriate surface water
routing scheme in hydrology models. Because of these ambiguities, we performed a simple test in
which the surface meltwater from Paxman et al.26 was added directly to the bed without seasonal
variability. Channel discharge volumes in this test increased, but the channel locations did not
change since surface melt was concentrated near the grounding line, where channels had already
formed. If, in the coming centuries, surface meltwater was to access the subglacial drainage
network, a more dynamic system reminiscent of the paleo ASB and West Greenland may form,
triggering highly variable grounding line positions and ice flow patterns, even in the absence of
MICI. We motivate future work to build on what we have shown here by investigating variability
in surface meltwater inputs to the bed, as this would provide insights into the stability of the ASB
drainage network in the face of perturbations to melt supply.”
Reviewer 3:
This is a very well written paper on changing Aurora subglacial basin drainage at different climate
states that is based on a finite-element glacier drainage system model which responds to climate
forcing through a link between ice thickness and water pressure at the bed. Using this methodology
forced today with BedMachine for the topography and ISMIP6 for the climate they simulate
potential drainage pattern under Totten which seems reasonable.
They then attempt similar situations at the Eocene-Oligocene boundary and at the mid-Miocene.
For the latter I think they are seeking to simulate the Mid-Miocene Climatic Optimum. There are
issues with specifically matching the O-18 curve with CO2 as the authors are undoubtedly aware,
but I don’t think this matters for the paper since you are forcing it at two CO2 states roughly
equivalent to E-O and MMCO. The specific date does not matter for your study since as noted
below, I don’t think you are yet able to simulate what specifically occurred with the ice sheet and
drainage system at the E-O and MMCO. The larger issues however are three:
1) bed topography has certainly evolved from the Eocene to today and thus what is the sensitivity
of the model to this process since we do not have a E-O or Mid-Mio bedmachine? There are some
sentences discussing how it might have changed but I was left unclear as the expected magnitude
and feedbacks if say the deeper basins under ASB we not yet filled in and we had a subglacier
lake scenario, or if the erosion through time has substantially changed the overall gradient to flatter
today than in the E-O run. Can we be confident of these glacial drainage change results in absence
of the topography? Some sensitivity study/discussion is needed to place these results in context on
this issue.
We thank the reviewer for raising these points about the bed topography. We realise we could have
been clearer about the sensitivity tests that we performed; Reviewer 1 also mentioned this (please
see our response to their comment above), and in the revised version of the manuscript, we have
now summarised the key findings from Text S1, which details the results of our sensitivity tests.
Below, we provide a review of these sensitivity tests.
Our first test investigated the sensitivity of drainage pathways to bed topography by keeping the
ice surface the same as in the source publication, but varying the bed topography, using either the
time-snapshot-specific bed topography or the modern BedMachine topography. For the paleo
simulations with the BedMachine basal topography, we found that channel lengths were affected,
but the main channel outlet locations remained the same.
In our second test, we kept the ice surface geometry the same as in the source publication but
varied the bed topography (using BedMachine), and modern-day basal velocities and meltwater
production rates (the “modern inputs” sensitivity test). The outputs from this test allowed us to
isolate the role of ice surface geometry in steering water flow. For the Eocene-Oligocene
Boundary, this test indicated that channelised drainage beneath Totten remains dominant,
highlighting the steep surface slopes during this time period. In contrast, drainage through Totten
is lower during the Mid-Miocene, which we attribute to weaker surface slopes. Despite the similar
drainage pathways to the runs with the time-snapshot specific data, the discharge volumes in the
modern inputs sensitivity test were lower than in the runs using time-snapshot-specific data.
Our final sensitivity test, which is a new addition to our manuscript based on comments from
Reviewer 1, investigated the role of variability in basal meltwater production rates. In this test, we
increased the modern basal meltwater production rate everywhere by a factor of 1.5, and applied
it to our paleo and future simulations while keeping the bed and ice geometries, as well as the
basal velocities, the same as those in the source publication. This test approximates the variability
in meltwater production that may result from ice sheet models whose physics differ from those in
the ice sheet models of Paxman et al. (2020) and Li et al. (2023). This test resulted in shorter and
less extensive channels with lower discharges than that of the standard setup, as well as a
reduction in the extent of high pressure regions. Overall, this test highlights the role that basal
meltwater production can have in subglacial drainage development and that tighter constraints
on this basal boundary condition are required.
Regarding the magnitude and feedbacks of bed topography changes, our subglacial hydrology
model is not coupled to erosion and solid earth models, as this is outside the scope of our work.
We are, therefore, unable to provide an estimate of the direction and magnitude of feedbacks
between solid earth uplift, erosional processes, and subglacial hydrology. However, we have
mentioned this limitation in the revised manuscript (L431-451) and in Text S3 of the supplementary
material (see responses to the above comments from Reviewer 2). We note, however, that the input
data from Paxman et al. (2020) did account for isostatic adjustment, erosion, sedimentation,
volcanism, and plate motions in their simulations.
2) The ice margin for the ASB portion of East Antarctica is not substantially changing between
the E-O, Mid-Mio, Today, and Future scenarios. There is certainly some retreat and some advance
aspects but these are way too small to match the offshore shelf and slope geophysical data implying
presence or absence of grounded ice (Gulick et al., 2017, Nature, Montelli et al. 2019 GSA
Bulletin, McKay et al., 2022, Ant Clim Evol). For instance, at the E-O boundary there were tunnel
valleys > 125 km seaward of the current ice margin which require grounded ice and we have a
glacial shelf crossing trough (Donda et al., 2020, Ant Sci; Hirano et al., 2023, Nature Comm)
reaching the shelf edge during the advances. There is strong data for grounded ice therefore over
much of the shelf and within the trough to the shelf edge since there is a large trough mouth fan
for the Totten system active in the Oligocene at least. Therefore your E-O simulation ice margin
should be substantially more advanced to match this geologic evidence. In counterpoint, there
appears to have been no evidence of proximal glacial sedimentary products in the MMCO on the
shelf and thus one would infer a much more retreated ice margin to explain this. Your Mid-Mio
simulation is somewhat retreated but probably far too little to explain the absence of glacial
sedimentary facies at the MMCO on the shelf.
We thank the reviewer for this comment. Reviewer 2 raised similar concerns, which we have
addressed above. Since we are not performing ice sheet modelling experiments, and our subglacial
hydrology model is supplied with data from Paxman et al. (2020), we are unable to change the
location of the grounding line. However, in the revised manuscript we have endeavoured to clarify
that the subglacial drainage systems we model are not intended to be “true” representations of
what the hydrology system looked like in the past but rather to provide a large-scale overview of
how changes in ice configurations and basal conditions influence Aurora Subglacial Basin’s
subglacial drainage system (L128-131):
“The purpose of these experiments is to provide a large-scale overview of how changes in ice
configurations and basal (melt, velocity, and topography) conditions influence Aurora Subglacial
Basin’s subglacial drainage system and are not intended to be interpreted as the exact subglacial
conditions during each of these paleo time snapshots.”
We have also commented on the role that coupled subglacial hydrology and ice dynamics
modelling may have in reproducing paleo grounding line positions (see L434-451 and the
responses to Reviewer 2’s comments above). We hope our findings will inspire such coupled
experiments to better represent ice extent during these time periods.
3) The lack of greater changes in ice margin at warmer and colder periods imply the current models
are missing some key feedbacks. It could be the effect of ice cliff instability as raised by the
authors. However another key change that should occur is going from colder to warmer based
glaciers such as is seen in north versus south Greenland outlet glaciers where warmer wetter ones
moving larger volumes of sediment potentially building glacial moraines or morainal banks, and are
correlated with tunnel valleys existing when advancing onto shelves (e.g., Alaska, North Sea).
Colder states act more like modern Antarctica or the colder based parts of Greenland forming
grounding zone wedges instead and substantially less feedbacks are likely. As Totten system
transitioned to this more polar state only the Late Miocene-Pliocene, it is probably incorrect to
assume the subglacial system worked the same way from a more modern polar state as it did in a
past more dynamic state. In other words E-O and Mid-Mio likely dynamically behaved more like
the North Sea or Alaska systems than Pleistocene Antarctica in order to explain the greatly
different shelf margin effects and glacial sedimentary products. What exactly is the change in
feedbacks is that allows for much more dynamic advance and retreat cycles is not yet known of
course but some combination of melt water, warm bases, and glacial sediment dynamics are likely
involved.
Moving forward with this paper I think the authors need to specifically note how the paleo model
runs do not produce dynamic enough advances to reach the shelf edge during the E-O or leave the
shelf entirely ice free during the Mid-Miocene and then discuss the possible additional feedbacks
needed to result in greater ice margin changes. Then discuss what effect this would have on the
subglacial networks that are the focus of this paper. In summary, this paper does a good job with
the paleo models if the bed topography did not differ substantially and if the glacial dynamics did
not change going into past climate states. Issue is we know the ice was a lot further advanced and
have evidence of a wetter more dynamic system that created tunnel valleys, trough mouth fans,
and probably intermittent morainal banks … how is this kind of system, one more representative
of the LGM Alaska, North Sea, or West Greenland for instance, differ from what is modeled in
this paper? Given there is clearly a mismatch in ice edge position with the geologic record at least
for maximum advance and retreat climate states, then how can we use this paper’s results to inform
us of process without yet being able to include all the processes required? I think the path forward
is to use the paleo model results to discuss how different inputs such as CO2 affect ice thickness
and water pressure and drainage without making the argument that this study is faithfully
reproducing the conditions at E-O and Mid-Mio. Consider what you models are not including and
how you might then frame your model results differently since its interesting the tradeoffs
observed in water pressure and drainage length in your work, and considering future scenarios (see
below), but these models clearly do not represent the state of the ASB glacial system at the E-O or
mid-Mio.
We thank the reviewer for raising these points. We’d like to emphasise that our work is exploratory
in nature, being the first to compare past, present, and future hydrology and ice shelf melt using
evolving 2-D models. Therefore, we are not attempting to recreate the exact conditions at each
time snapshot. We do, however, agree that acknowledging the limitations of our modelling
approach is important for framing the results and their implications, and reviewer 2 raised similar
concerns about our modelled system and that suggested by the paleo record. In the discussion of
our revised manuscript and in Text S3, we have noted the discrepancies between our modelling
results and observations. We have now provided suggestions for future work such that a closer
match between model outputs and geomorphological evidence can be obtained. We have
addressed the role of solid earth uplift, surface meltwater and erosion processes in the region and
motivated the use of coupled ice sheet-hydrology models as this may lead to grounding line
locations more representative of those documented in the paleo record. We hope these
amendments, along with our clarification of the aim and intention of this manuscript, have satisfied
these concerns.
For the future model runs, I think these are fine and in fact really interesting suggestions for future
states, if the system stays in its current polar mode of dynamics. However, if it switches modes to
the way it operated in the Oligocene to Miocene then there would be expected a much greater
dynamic change possibility that could be acknowledged.
We thank the reviewer for the positive feedback, and we have now made this comparison in the
revised version (L424-427):
“If, in the coming centuries, surface meltwater were to access the subglacial drainage network,
a more dynamic system reminiscent of the paleo ASB and West Greenland may form, triggering
highly variable grounding line positions and ice flow patterns, even in the absence of MICI.”
On the writing, this paper is remarkably free of typos, has excellently written sentences, and was
very clear to read. Only minor item on that front is that the word further (a concept) is used in two
places where the word should be farther (a distance).
We have made this correction.
My recommendation is therefore Major Revisions to consider the issues with mismatch to the
geologic record and suggestions of glacial dynamics having a warmer wetter regime with processes
not yet included in the finite glacial drainage system modeling.
Hopefully this review will be helpful and I would be willing to do a re-review as needed,
Sean Gulick

### Reviewer 3

This is a revised submission of a very interesting and well written modeling study by Hayden et al on the effects of subglacial hydrology on ice sheet dynamics in the Aurora subglacial basin, East Antarctica. In general, I accept a lot of the response to reviewers aspects that the authors raised and appreciate the edited discussion in the main text and supplemental.
However, I recommend an additional minor set of edits which are a suggestion to be more specific in the caveats starting with line 430. Right now the paper lumps the geological evidence under the terminology "geomorphologic evidence" (or some variant) which is partly correct but misses also the glacial sequence stratigraphy on the shelf (i.e. the geologic record) published in several of the papers you cite in this section. So I strongly recommend not just mentioning that the modeling of ice extents is known to be inconsistent with shelf morphology (e.g. presence of a shelf crossing trough and lateral moraines) during ice advances, but also note that it is inconsistent with presence of stratigraphic indicators of grounded ice (e.g. tunnel valleys and sedimentary deposits) both for the advanced and retreated positions of the ASB marine terminating ice. I understand ice extents are baked into the boundary conditions of your model so you cannot change this aspect, but you can make it clear that your modeling therefore greatly under-predicts the terminus response due warm states (e.g. the MMCO) and cold states (e.g. E/O boundary) and a more complete list of the key factors/feedbacks could matter and need to be integrated into future studies. For instance I recommend adding in that one key feedback not included within this modeling or in Paxman et al is the role of subglacial sediments in addition to subglacial hydrology. For instance your long hydrologic conduits very likely should become tunnel valleys in the model with a feedback built in that these are erosive sub glacially but depositional near the terminus and thus can provide a direct feedback to the ground line stability, which likely then changes under different flow regimes/with connection to surface melt/with different hydrologic pressures (as you note). I don't think you can ignore the role of erosion/redistribution of sediment within the subglacial hydrologic system and so should at least include this within the discussion as to potential reasons why the ice terminus is not as responsive as the geologic record has evidence for and help bridge the gap between the current modeling of a stable terminus (despite lots of mass balance changes) and what the geologic record indicates. For instance in 470-474, could add "with changes to the bed and sediment redistribution being a potentially important feedback".
