Then provide a 2–3 sentence rationale explaining your prediction.

## Paper

## Abstract

Aurora Subglacial Basin (ASB) in East Antarctica is among the most rapidly changing regions in Antarctica. Beneath the ASB, subglacial drainage networks allow for fast ice flow and facilitate mass losses by eroding the coastal ice shelves. The ASB underwent advance-retreat cycles since its inception 34 million years ago, and projections rely on these findings to predict future ice behaviour. Yet, these hindcasts and forecasts seldom consider the effects of subglacial drainage. Here, we model subglacial drainage networks and ice shelf basal melting of the ASB from 34 million years ago to 2100 CE. Our results indicate continual reorganisation of ASB drainage systems and ice shelf melt patterns, suggesting that the past does not fully serve as an analogue for the future. Since subglacial drainage accounts for up to 70% of ice shelf melt, our results imply that subglacial hydrology could trigger higher rates of mass loss than previously suggested.

---

## Introduction

Ongoing climate warming has signalled concern about the fate of the Antarctic Ice Sheet and future sea levels, especially since the East Antarctic Ice Sheet contains 52 m of potential sea level rise1, the largest of all modern-day ice reservoirs. Within East Antarctica, Totten Glacier, in the Aurora Subglacial Basin (ASB, Fig. 1), is rapidly changing, displaying both the highest grounded ice thinning rates and highest rates of ice discharge of all East Antarctic outlet glaciers2. This area contains an ice volume equivalent of 3.9 m of sea level rise1 and is currently in a state of negative mass balance3. In recent decades, Totten Glacier has experienced periods of accelerated ice flow velocities, ice thinning, and grounding line retreat2–8. These changes are associated with intrusions of warm, modified Circumpolar Deep Water5,7–10 (mCDW), which erodes Totten Glacier’s Ice Shelf, the floating portion of Totten Glacier that serves as a girdle on ice flow.

Totten Glacier and the ASB may be inherently unstable due to a large proportion of the ice in the region grounded below sea level on a reverse bed slope1,11, making it susceptible to the Marine Ice Sheet Instability12 (MISI). Furthermore, collapse of buttressing ice shelves and unstoppable grounding line retreat may occur if the Marine Ice Cliff Instability (MICI) is set in motion due to ice shelf hydrofracture and ice cliff failure13. Models that include MICI suggest some of the highest projected ice loss and sea level rise estimates, but since there is limited observational evidence of past MICI behaviour14 and large uncertainties in MICI processes15, the plausibility of MICI continues to be debated. In the ASB, including MICI in modelled projections can cause thousands of square kilometres of grounded ice to be lost (Fig. S7). Regardless of the potential impacts of MICI, it is likely that mCDW will continue to affect ASB’s glaciers over the next century and push grounding lines farther inland, with the magnitude and extent of this retreat dependent on greenhouse gas emissions16. This situation could be exacerbated if instability mechanisms were to be initiated. Still, since most ice sheet models neglect evolving subglacial hydrology, it has seldom been considered that changes to subglacial drainage systems may be sufficient to initiate large-scale ice dynamic and geometric changes without the need for MICI.

The future trajectory of ice loss in ASB could potentially resemble that from the geologic past when climate conditions were similar to those predicted for the coming decades and centuries13,17. It has been suggested that the dynamic behaviour of the paleo-ASB can partially be explained by the subglacial drainage network configuration18–20. Present-day subglacial drainage in the ASB consists of a network of long, high-pressure channels that reach far into the interior of the ASB21. These channels play a critical role in regulating the flow of the overlying ice, while also pumping large volumes of freshwater beneath ice shelves, facilitating high and localised ice shelf basal melt rates22. If the volume of discharge exiting these channels, or their locations, were to change, there could be far-reaching impacts on the stability of ice flow in the ASB, such as accelerations of ice velocities and grounding line retreat rates23. However, there has not been a focused study on evolving subglacial drainage in the ASB during previous warm periods, how hydrology will be configured in future warm conditions, and the associated consequences of these changes for ice dynamics and ice shelf basal melt rates.

Here, we use the 2D, finite-element Glacier Drainage System24 (GlaDS, described in Methods) subglacial hydrology model to assess how ice sheet geometry at different time snapshots in the past and future affect the subglacial hydrology of the ASB’s grounded ice and infer the effects on ice shelf basal melt rates. We consider different concentrations of greenhouse gases and the impact of the MICI mechanism on the channel network and drainage system pressurisation. We show that there has been substantial reorganisation of the ASB’s basal hydrological networks since the inception of the Antarctic Ice Sheet 34 million years ago, and that drainage will continue to evolve over the next century in response to climate warming.

---

## Results

Present-day subglacial hydrology
We first simulate modern-day subglacial hydrology using bed topography from BedMachine Antarctica1 and basal velocities and meltwater production rates from the Ice Sheet Model Intercomparison Project for CMIP6 (ISMIP625). With these datasets, we have revised and expanded the domain used in Dow et al.21 to capture up glacier activity and facilitate the comparison between our paleo and future simulations. Since Dow et al.’s21 model outputs were validated by radar-derived specularity content data, we consider their model outputs to be a benchmark for our model runs. We therefore adopt the same parameter values as used in Dow et al.’s21 base model run for bedrock obstacle sizes and distributed and channelised system conductivities. Like in Dow et al.21, we find that channel discharges are greatest through Totten Glacier, with fluxes reaching 33 m3 s-1 from the entire section of Totten’s grounding line (Fig. 2c). High water pressure occurs in the upland regions, another similarity between our simulations and those in Dow et al.21. Due to the high level of agreement between our modern-day results and those of Dow et al.’s21, the remainder of this paper focuses on how paleo and future subglacial hydrology compares to the contemporary drainage system. We direct readers to Dow et al.21 for an in-depth analysis of the present-day drainage system of the ASB.

Paleo subglacial hydrology
Our paleo subglacial hydrology simulations use grounding lines, ice sheet geometries, and basal inputs from Paxman et al.26. We focus on the Eocene-Oligocene Boundary (34 Mya) and the Mid-Miocene Climate Transition (14 Mya; hereafter Mid-Miocene) as these intervals correspond to ice volumes in ASB that are larger and smaller, respectively, than those in the present day26. The purpose of these experiments is to provide a large-scale overview of how changes in ice configurations and basal (melt, velocity, and topography) conditions influence ASB’s subglacial drainage system and are not intended to be interpreted as the exact subglacial conditions during each of these paleo time snapshots. In the Discussion, we compare our model results to geomorphological evidence.

Here, we focus on the subglacial hydrology and ice shelf basal melting results produced by adopting the ice geometries from Paxman et al.’s26 “No MICI, 500 ppm CO2” experiments. This level of CO2 represents (a) the likely lower bound during the Eocene-Oligocene Boundary, (b) the likely upper bound for the Mid-Miocene, and (c) the possible CO2 concentration for the future27–34. Due to limited observational evidence and divided findings from modelling efforts, is not yet clear if MICI has occurred in the geologic past and if it will occur in the next centuries14,15. We discuss how the ice geometries from Paxman et al.’s26 MICI and low CO2 experiments affect our results in the section titled “Carbon emissions and instability processes influence drainage morphology”.

Our Eocene-Oligocene Boundary results indicate that channels grew up to 370 km long (Fig. 2a), more than twice the length of present-day channels in the ASB (Fig. 2c and Dow et al.21). Nearly 160 m3 s-1 of channelised discharge exits the subglacial drainage system at the grounding line, shared between 9 outlet channels. 95% of this discharge is sourced from channels draining across Totten Glacier’s grounding line rather than the nearby Vanderford and Bond Glaciers. One of Totten’s channels pumps 117 m3 s-1 of freshwater into the ice shelf cavity, accounting for 75% of ASB’s cumulative grounding line discharge. Discharge from this channel alone exceeds the cumulative grounding line discharge from ASB’s current drainage system by 40 m3 s-1. All channels are fed by regions with water around ice overburden pressure. However, channels do not substantially reduce water pressure, and are within 5% of ice overburden pressure, consistent with modelling of present-day channels21. 95.47% of the domain is at or above 95% of ice overburden pressure; the highest proportion of all simulations.

We find a close correspondence with high pressure regions (Fig. 3) and thick (≥0.08 m) water sheets. These thicker sheets tend to be in basal troughs (Fig. S1) and show agreement with the up glacier initiation points of small channels. We do not observe an overlap between large water sheet thicknesses and high basal velocities or basal meltwater production rates. Since we do not couple our subglacial hydrology model to an ice sheet model, we use the basal meltwater production rates and basal velocities determined by Paxman et al.26 as inputs into our model. The highest velocities occur beneath Totten Glacier, which we capped at 800 m a-1 to prevent model instabilities (Table S1). Basal meltwater production rates beneath Totten Glacier reach 2 m a-1 at the grounding line, which is nearly six times larger than the present-day meltwater production rate at the grounding line21. Meltwater production remains elevated (≥10 cm a-1) up to 160 km from the grounding line, beyond which it approaches the catchment-wide mean of 6 mm a-1, exceeding the present-day catchment-wide average by 2.3 mm a-1. Overall, these results suggest spatially-variable controls on drainage beneath ASB. Topographic controls and basal melting have a greater influence on subglacial drainage up glacier, whereas high basal velocities and meltwater production rates play a dominant role in drainage morphology beneath Totten Glacier and closer to the grounding line. We performed sensitivity tests to determine the relative influence of bed and surface topography, basal melt, and basal velocity (Text S1). These tests indicated that the ice surface geometry is the primary control on where dominant drainage pathways form, but that changes in bed topography can influence channel lengths. Varying basal meltwater production rates and velocities caused more than a 10-fold change in grounding line channel fluxes and changes in the distribution and extent of high-pressure regions, both of which can affect ice dynamics through their influence ice shelf basal melt rates and on ice velocities, respectively.

In the Mid-Miocene, similar to the Eocene-Oligocene Boundary, high water pressures and thick water sheets are coincident and form in basal troughs. The largest channels also occur where basal velocities and rates of basal meltwater production are highest. Beyond this, the subglacial drainage morphology during the Mid-Miocene differs substantially from that at the Eocene-Oligocene Boundary. For instance, the maximum channel length for the Mid-Miocene is 270 km long (Fig. 2b), 100 km shorter than the longest channel in our Eocene-Oligocene runs (although ~100 km longer than present-day channels; Fig. 2c and Dow et al.21). The Mid-Miocene channels pump 35 m3 s-1 less water across the grounding line than the channels in the Eocene-Oligocene drainage system. However, there are more channels crossing the grounding line in the Mid-Miocene run since the ice in this simulation has retreated past Law Dome. This pattern of ice retreat results in a grounding line channel density (number of channels per km of grounding line) that is ~3.4 times higher than that of the Eocene-Oligocene Boundary. This suggests that retreat past Law Dome can trigger, or at least contribute to, reorganisation of water flow, as well as determining where the majority of the water exits the domain. We find that during the Mid-Miocene, discharge over the section of grounding line near Totten Glacier is relatively small compared to our Eocene-Oligocene simulations, and accounts for only a third of the total grounding line discharge. During the Mid-Miocene, our results indicate that the largest discharge crossing the grounding line occurs near the former location of Law Dome. Across this section of the grounding line, the maximum channel discharge is ~29 m3 s-1, with a cumulative channel discharge of 58.29 m3 s-1 in this region, which accounts for nearly half of the total channelised grounding line discharge.

Future subglacial hydrology
We next investigate the possible subglacial drainage morphologies of the ASB at 2100 CE, using ice geometries from Li et al.35, who considered how the spectrum of CMIP6 climate forcing impacts Antarctic Ice Sheet evolution. We selected the Li et al.35 ice geometries from CMIP6 forcings that resulted in the greatest ice loss (NorESM2-MM) and the largest ice gain (CMCC-CM2-SR5), representing end-member scenarios for ASB. Similar to our paleo experiments, we run two sets of simulations for each CMIP6 forcing, one in which the ice geometry was generated with MICI processes turned on, and one where these processes were excluded. The results from the MICI runs are presented in the supplementary information.

The degree of similarity of future subglacial drainage to present or past drainage networks is highly dependent on ice surface slope changes. For the maximum ice gain scenario, grounding line channel discharge at 2100 CE (Fig. 2e) is of a similar magnitude to the present (Fig. 2c, Table S3 and Dow et al.21) and has similar grounding line channel density. However, channels are up to 100 km longer in this future scenario. Under high rates of ice loss (Fig. 2d), channel length (303 km), discharges (163 m3 s-1), and grounding line channel density (0.0108 channels per km of groundling line) resemble that of the Eocene-Oligocene Boundary, albeit the organisation of the drainage system is more branching in the future simulation. These channel lengths, discharges, and densities are more than twice that of the present-day. For both future scenarios, most of the discharge exits at the grounding lines of Moscow University Ice Shelf and Totten Glaciers. However, while Totten Glacier accounted for three-quarters of total discharge during the Eocene-Oligocene Boundary, at 2100 CE, it only accounts for 35% of the grounding line discharge. This suggests that the changes in ice and bed geometry over time favour a more arborescent channelised drainage network. Furthermore, relative to the present-day simulation, we find that the partitioning of drainage in both of our future simulations tends to favour greater discharges beneath Bond and Vanderford Glaciers.

We find substantial differences between the channel discharges for the two future scenarios. The maximum ice loss scenario results in more than twice the channel density and discharge at the grounding line compared to the maximum ice gain scenario (0.0108 channels per km of groundling line for the maximum ice loss scenario versus 0.0053 channels per km of grounding line for the maximum ice gain scenario). The discharge velocity (channel flux divided by channel cross-sectional area) of the largest channel from the maximum ice loss scenario is 0.9741 m s-1, >30% faster than that observed in the maximum ice gain scenario (0.6347 m s-1) and >40 times faster than that from the Eocene-Oligocene (0.0233 m s-1). The steep surface slopes of the maximum ice loss run, especially near the grounding line, lead to higher hydraulic potential gradients (Fig. S13) that cause high basal velocities and meltwater production rates. Consequently, discharge volumes and associated water velocities are much larger than the others simulations, which drive enhanced rates of ice shelf basal melting at deep grounding line points by locally increasing rates of turbulent sub-ice shelf ocean mixing near the discharge outflow locations. We discuss these implications in the section titled “Ice shelf basal melt impacts”.

Similar to our paleo and present-day runs, our water pressure results for the future runs indicate that high pressures continue to persist in basal depressions. Compared to the paleo simulations, the region where water pressures reach or exceed ice overburden pressure (yellow contours in Fig. 3) has migrated further inland. These upland regions of over-pressured troughs do not occur in the present-day run. It is likely that erosion of the bed since the Eocene-Oligocene Boundary has heightened ASB’s sensitivity to climate-driven retreat26. Our simulations indicate that these bed changes over time have also influenced the distribution of subglacial water pressures and primary subglacial drainage pathways and support the findings of Wright et al.36 who suggested that a basal trough that meanders inland and near Totten Glacier connects up glacier subglacial drainage to the downstream drainage system. Our results show that pressures remain above overburden in the upland region, which, if using water pressure as a proxy for ice velocity, suggests that fast velocities may migrate further inland in the future.

Carbon emissions and instability processes influence drainage morphology
We also tested how paleo ice configurations that resulted from lower CO2 levels affected our outputs (Figs. S14–S21). Channels in our low (280 ppm) CO2 simulations were up to 37 km shorter than those from the 500 ppm simulations, with nearly 60 m3 s-1 less total grounding line discharge. Since the ice has not retreated as far back in the low CO2 simulations (Figs. S14–S15), the grounding line channel density is lower. This difference is most prominent in the Mid-Miocene 280 ppm No MICI run, where the grounding line channel density is half that of the 500 ppm simulation. Mean channel pressure in our low CO2 No MICI runs is also slightly lower (by up to 1.5%) than in our 500 ppm No MICI runs. However, the channel pressures are still within 95% of ice overburden, as in present-day Antarctic channels. This suggests that the effect of channels on ice-bed coupling in our paleo simulations is independent of the CO2 concentration. However, two-way coupled simulations of ice dynamics and hydrology are necessary to determine if this is the case. Similar to our 500 ppm simulations, thick and overpressured water sheets form in basal troughs. In the Eocene 280 ppm run, there is a lower proportion of the domain (54.7%) at and above 98% of ice overburden, compared to the 500 ppm run (58.48%). However, in the Mid-Miocene run, the opposite is true – raising the CO2 concentration lowers the percent of the domain at high pressure, from 49% in the 500 ppm run to 43.7% in the 280 ppm run.

The runs in which the ice geometries were influenced by MICI show considerable departures from the No MICI runs. In the MICI runs, grounding line channel densities were higher, channels tended to be shorter, and channel overburden pressures were lower than those in the No MICI runs. For the paleo runs, these results suggest that, in the absence of MICI processes, variability in CO2 concentrations can substantially affect subglacial drainage networks. This is likely because the steeper surface slopes in the higher-CO2 run cause steeper hydraulic potential gradients, resulting in longer channels. While MICI also tends to steepen ice surface, and therefore, hydraulic gradients, we do not observe longer channels in the paleo MICI runs compared to the No MICI runs because the grounding line has retreated much farther back in the runs where MICI is included. This pattern is not generalisable for our future simulations. While we do see shorter channels in the maximum ice loss MICI run, the maximum ice gain MICI simulation resulted in a maximum channel length of 308.73 km, more than 60 km longer than that of the corresponding No MICI run, and the longest channel of all the future runs. To investigate this further, we analysed the ratio of hydraulic potential gradients. In the MICI run, the ratio of hydraulic gradients for maximum ice loss to maximum ice gain is much more similar than in the No MICI runs. This is because the much steeper ice surface slopes in the maximum ice gain MICI run result in steeper hydraulic potential gradients. Relative to its respective No MICI simulation, the hydraulic gradients of the maximum ice gain MICI run are up to two times steeper. Therefore, we attribute the longer channels in the maximum ice gain MICI run to its steeper hydraulic gradients. Text S2 further discusses the interplay between ice geometry and hydraulic gradient.

We also found that the differences between total grounding line discharges in the No MICI versus MICI scenario were dependent on the time snapshot. In the paleo simulations, MICI lowered the total volume of grounding line discharge, with the largest decrease observed in the Mid-Miocene run, where discharges were 2.6 times lower in the MICI run compared to the No MICI run. In the future runs, however, incorporating MICI led to increases in channel discharge. While this increase was relatively small for the maximum ice loss run (3 m3 s-1), channel discharges in the maximum ice gain scenario increased nearly three-fold. The total channelised discharge volume in the maximum ice gain run with MICI run was the largest of all simulations considered, amounting to 198 m3 s-1. Taken together, our results highlight how MICI can substantially influence the drainage system. We motivate future work to build on what we have presented here by using coupled models that allow for evolving subglacial drainage and ice dynamics, as well as the option for MICI to be switched on and off. In doing so, a complete picture of how variations in subglacial drainage influence ice dynamics, and vice versa, will be obtained.

Ice shelf basal melt impacts
Subglacial outflow across Antarctic grounding lines and into sub-ice shelf ocean cavities has been posited to locally enhance ice shelf basal melting by both enhancing turbulence of the near-grounding line water mass and enhancing buoyancy of sub-ice shelf plumes that drive melting22,37,38. Using an ice shelf basal melt parameterisation that resolves melt driven by ocean circulation and subglacial freshwater outflow (Pelle et al.39; see Methods), we assess the sensitivity of ice shelf melt rates to the modelled paleo, modern, and future subglacial conditions discussed above. Parameterised ice shelf melt enhancements from subglacial freshwater outflow are strong but highly localised (Fig. 4). In the 500 ppm No MICI paleo simulations, the ice shelf melt enhancement at the Eocene-Oligocene Boundary (maximum enhancement of 38.43 m a-1) has a higher magnitude and is more spatially concentrated than the melt enhancement at the Mid-Miocene (maximum enhancement of 16.23 m a-1) due to the varying configurations of the subglacial channels draining across the grounding lines. In both paleo experiments, these melt enhancements comprise up to 70% of the total grounding line melt signal adjacent to the discharge channel (Fig. S32). In modern and future simulations, along Totten Glacier’s southern grounding zone, small changes in the subglacial channel distribution lead to considerable changes in the downstream limit of the ice shelf melt enhancement (5L’, see Methods), which reaches a maximum distance of 5.83 km, 10.04 km and 17.72 km in the modern, maximum ice gain, and maximum ice loss experiments, respectively. As ice shelf geometry and ocean conditions are consistent across these experiments, differences in the downstream limit of these melt enhancements are solely caused by differences in the configuration of the subglacial channels at the grounding line (i.e. fluxes and channel widths). In the modern, future maximum ice gain, and future maximum ice loss runs, subglacial outflow leads to enhanced ice shelf basal mass loss of 0.65 Gt, 2.23 Gt, and 3.62 Gt over the Totten Ice Shelf, respectively, and 0.21 Gt, 1.07 Gt, and 0.23 Gt over the Vanderford and Adams ice shelves, respectively (total basal mass loss over the Totten and Vanderford/Adams ice shelves in lieu of discharge are 178.44 Gt and 24.80 Gt, respectively). Although the magnitude of these shelf-integrated discharge-driven ice shelf melt enhancements seems inconsequential, these enhancements comprise up to 30% of the total Totten Ice Shelf grounding line melt signal in modern and maximum ice gain and up to 50% in maximum ice loss scenarios. Melt enhancements of Vincennes Bay outlet glaciers exhibit strong sensitivity to the simulated discharge conditions. Melt enhancements in the modern run are minimal due to the small amounts of simulated discharge (Fig. 4k); however, in 2100 (simulations with a more developed subglacial hydrology system) melt enhancements peak at 58.40 m a-1 and 25.64 m a-1 near the Vanderford and Adams grounding lines in maximum ice gain and maximum ice loss scenarios, respectively (Fig. 4l, m). We further explore the sensitivity of 2100 CE ice shelf melting of Vincennes Bay outlet glaciers (pink box in Fig. 4d) to subglacial hydrology model inputs of basal water production, ice velocity, and bed topography for the No MICI maximum ice gain runs (Fig. S33). Melt enhancements reach peak values near the southern limit of the Vanderford Ice Shelf and the Adams Ice Shelf in the modern bed topography experiment (Fig. S33a) and modern inputs experiment (Fig. S33c), respectively, owing to the differing distribution of grounding line discharge between these simulations. We note that in a complementary study, Pelle et al.23 developed a coupled ISSM-GlaDS configuration of ASB and, in projections to 2100, found that subglacial discharge-driven melt enhancements led to earlier onset of retreat of Totten Glacier’s southern grounding zone by ~25 years and continually accelerated retreat of Vanderford Glacier (up to 10 km of additional retreat compared to uncoupled “ISSM-only” simulations). That is, while the magnitude of these discharge melt enhancements is small relative to the background ocean-driven melt signal, their location at deep grounding line points has cascading impacts on the upstream stress regime of entire glacial basins. As such, the highly sensitive nature of the melt enhancements presented here highlights the importance of better constraining subglacial hydrology model inputs and boundary conditions, which will, in turn, improve simulations of past, present, and future ice sheet dynamics.

---

## Methods

Subglacial hydrology modelling
For our subglacial hydrology simulations, we use the Glacier Drainage System (GlaDS) model24. GlaDS is a 2D finite-element model that allows for the co-evolution of distributed and channelised drainage over grounded ice. Distributed drainage is approximated as linked cavities that form on elements of a triangular mesh, which exchange water along element edges where channels form. Rather than being specified at the beginning of the run, these channels develop over the simulation time as fluxes and pressures evolve in the distributed system. The equation describing channel evolution is given by:

∂S/∂t = (Ξ/ρL) - (ASjNjn-1N) (1)

where S is the channel cross-sectional area, Ξ is the viscous dissipation of potential energy, Π describes the sensible heat changes due to changes in pressure melting point, ρi is the ice density, L is the latent heat of fusion, N is the effective pressure within the channel. A and n are empirically-derived constants, with the former relating to ice temperature, and the latter to and strain rate.

Although channels can form on any element edge within the domain, we restrict our analysis to channels with discharges >0.5 m3 s-1. To prevent model instabilities, we limit the maximum channel cross-sectional area to 500 m2. Close correspondence between GlaDS outputs (e.g., channel outlet locations and ponded water) and remotely sensed present-day basal conditions in East and West Antarctica suggests that the model is ideal for our investigation of paleo and future subglacial hydrology21,50–52.

We constructed 13 domains, one for each of the ice sheet configurations (8 for the paleo simulations, 1 for the present-day simulation, and 4 for the future simulations) considered in our study. These domains were determined by assuming that the subglacial water pressure is equal to ice overburden pressure. Since hydraulic potential analysis is based on the geometry of the ice and bed, the source data in this calculation influence the flow routing and, therefore, the domain size. From here, we construct our meshes, which are restricted to ~20,000 nodes due to computational limitations. We do not have refined regions in the meshes. In Table S1, we summarise key characteristics of the domains and the boundary conditions (e.g., the number of nodes, mesh edge lengths, maximum ice surface and bed elevation, basal water input rates, and basal velocities). We run the model up to steady-state over 30,000 days. Steady state is reached when the distributed water sheet thickness differs by <10-7 m day-1 between two consecutive timesteps21,50,53. After reaching steady state, we run the model for another 10,000 days. Results in the main text show the model outputs at the end of these 10,000 days. At this point, the sheet thickness differences between the two final timesteps range from 2.2 × 10-8 m day-1 to 8.52 × 10-7 m day-1 and are therefore within our criterion for reaching steady state.

GlaDS requires ice surface and basal topography, basal meltwater production rates (due to geothermal and frictional heating) and basal velocities as inputs. These data come from Paxman et al.26 for the paleo simulations, BedMachine Antarctica1 and initMIP-Antarctica25 for present day, and Li et al.35 for the future runs. We have summarised the range of values for these inputs in Table S1.

As mentioned in the main text, we selected paleo time snapshots when ice configurations in the ASB were larger (Eocene-Oligocene Boundary) and smaller (Mid-Miocene) than present day. These data are from Paxman et al.26, who explored the sensitivity of Antarctic Ice Sheet evolution to climate changes. Their experiments forced an ice sheet model with CO2 concentrations of either 280 ppm or 500 ppm, allowing MICI to be turned on or off. Using the Paxman et al. ice sheet model outputs as inputs to the GlaDS model, we consider all possible combinations for each time snapshot: 280 ppm without MICI, 280 ppm with MICI, 500 ppm without MICI, and 500 ppm with MICI. This resulted in a total of 8 simulations (4 for the Eocene-Oligocene Boundary, and 4 for the Mid-Miocene). Li et al.35 forced their ice sheet model with the 36 CMIP6 models available at the time of their publication. Since guidelines for selecting CMIP6 models for ice sheet modelling and analysis were unavailable at the time of writing, we select a subset of the model outputs from Li et al.35 based on a regional analysis of their performance over the ASB. Grounding line retreat distance was not an informative metric since the models showed the same grounding line locations for 2100, likely due to the coarse resolution of the models. Despite the similarities in grounding line locations, the patterns of ice loss and gain varied greatly between models. We, therefore, use the metric of total ice thickness difference at 2100 relative to 2020 over the ASB for the No MICI simulations. NorESM2-MM resulted in the largest ice loss, while CMCC-CM2-SR5 resulted in the greatest ice thickness gain over the ASB. These models therefore represent the endmembers for ice geometry change over the ASB based on Li et al.’s35 outputs. We also use the MICI complement of this subset of Li et al.35 model outputs, for a total of 4 future model runs.

The results presented in the main manuscript adopt the GlaDS parameter values that resulted in the closest agreement between present day hydrological modelling and remotely-sensed observations in the ASB21. These values are summarised in Table S2 in the supplement. In the Supplementary Material, we include the results of our sensitivity tests (Figs. S22–23 and Text S1). We focused on basal meltwater production rates, basal velocity, and basal topography. We ran simulations where we set the basal topography to that of BedMachine Antarctica1, but use the ice surface geometry, basal velocity, and basal melt data from the source publication. Since, in this test, we are only changing the bed topography but keeping everything else the same as in the source publication, it allows us to determine the level of control that basal topography has on the subglacial drainage system. Although the ice surface slope is known to exert a dominant influence on large-scale subglacial drainage40, water flow paths are also sensitive to basal topography54–56, with rerouting and water piracy possible under slight variations in bed topography54–56. Furthermore, large changes in bed slopes over relatively short distances can cause freeze-on as basal water moves from a region of high to low pressure; this effect has been incorporated in GlaDS57. Thus, our bed topography test allows us to examine the persistence and sensitivity of subglacial drainage pathways to bed geometry. Our second sensitivity test imposes modern-day values for basal topography, basal velocity and basal meltwater production to all model runs while keeping the ice surface geometry the same as in the source publication. This allows us to assess the role of ice surface topography on the drainage system evolution. Our final test examines the role of meltwater production rates by increasing the modern-day initMIP25 basal water production rates by a factor of 1.5, while keeping the basal velocities and ice and basal geometries the same as in the source publication. This provides an approximation of how melt could vary for ice sheet geometries governed by different ice sheet model physics.

Ice shelf basal melt parameterisation
For each subglacial hydrology simulation, we compute melting driven by sub-ice shelf ocean circulation and grounding line subglacial discharge with the buoyant plume parameterisation developed by Pelle et al.39. This parameterisation, based on the theory of buoyant sub-ice shelf plumes, applies a meltwater plume model58 that is modified near grounding line subglacial outflow locations to account for discharge-enhanced ice shelf melt using a discharge plume model37. The meltwater plume model simulates plumes that originate at the grounding line and travel upward along the base of the ice shelf, inducing melt up to the ice front or to the point at which the current loses buoyancy. The plume’s trajectory is controlled primarily by the ambient ocean temperature and salinity (Ta and Sa, respectively), the local slope angle of the ice shelf draft (α), and the depth the plume originated that reaches a particular shelf point (grounding line depth, zgl). Within a prescribed distance away from grounding line subglacial discharge locations, melt rates additionally become proportional to the grounding line subglacial freshwater flux (qsg) to the one-third power37,59. This distance (5L’, metres) that sets the cutoff between the meltwater and discharge plume models is set as a radius around grounding line discharge locations and is governed by the following equation:

5L’ = (500 * qsg^(2/3)) / (g * Δρi * C1 * Γ * Ts0 * G1 * G2 * λ3 * ΔTf,gl) (2)

where qsg^(2/3) is the grounding line subglacial discharge flux (m2 s-1), g is Earth’s gravitational constant (9.80 m s-2), Δρi is the density contrast between the plume and ambient ocean waters, C1=2Γ is a heat exchange parameter (6 * 10-4), G1 and G2 are geometric terms that provide melt rates the proper scaling to the slope angle of the ice shelf draft and grounding line depth field, and λ3 * ΔTf,gl is a measure of the ocean thermal forcing (°C). Given inputs of Ta, Sa, α, zgl, and qsg, the melt rate parameterisation outputs an ice shelf basal melt rate field that resolves melting driven by both large-scale ocean circulation and localised subglacial discharge. Note that melt enhancements from subglacial discharge were computed by differencing melt fields that were computed with qsg taken from GlaDS and with qsg set to zero.

Input ice shelf geometries (providing α and zgl) for both paleo, modern, and future subglacial hydrology simulations are consistent with the descriptions in the above subglacial hydrology modelling methods section. Input ocean conditions (Ta = -0.73 °C, Sa = 34.73 units on the practical salinity scale) for the 280 ppm paleo, modern, and future simulations were obtained by averaging observed60 bottom ocean temperature and salinity along the Sabrina Coast. For the 500 ppm paleo simulations, we apply 5 °C ocean warming to remain consistent with Paxman et al.26 and do not change the salinity (i.e., Ta = 4.27 °C and Sa = 34.73 units on the practical salinity scale).

Data availability
The subglacial hydrology model outputs and ice shelf basal melt rates generated in this study are available from the Zenodo repository: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.14014169. Source data are provided with this paper.

Code availability
The Glacier Drainage System (GlaDS) model code is available from Mauro Werder (werder@vaw.baug.ethz.ch). GlaDS is also now implemented in the open-access Ice-sheet and Sea-level System Model (https://issm.jpl.nasa.gov/). The melt rate parameterization used in this study is published in Pelle et al.39 and uses the model outputs provided in the data submission.

### Reviewer 2

I read this well-prepared and clearly written manuscript with great interest because there is compelling geomorphologic
evidence to suggest that subglacial meltwater, either from the drainage of subglacial lakes or surface melting, may be
influencing/may have influenced ice dynamics in the ASB throughout the Cenozoic. As such, modeling studies are required
to assess the potential impact of subglacial meltwater presence on ice behavior during past warm periods, particularly in the
Totten Glacier catchment, where thinning and ice mass loss and an active subglacial hydrologic system are presently
observed.
Two past time intervals were chosen as part of this study to reflect times when 1) regional ice volume was larger than at
present with higher pCO2 (E-O boundary) and 2) possibly smaller than present with who knows what pCO2 (Middle
Miocene). At least I think this was the goal because the introduction talks about needing to understand how the subglacial
hydrologic system worked during past warm periods. However, the intervals listed are those of glacial expansion. Climate at
the EO boundary was relatively cold, and if the goal of the middle Miocene study was to hit the Miocene Climate Optimum,
the warmest time interval of the last 30 Ma, that date and ice sheet configuration should reflect ~16 Ma and not ~14 Ma,
when ice expanded and stabilized. The authors conclude that there have been substantial reorganizations of the subglacial
drainage system over ~40 million years. Well yes, this seems like a pretty safe takeaway for a manuscript.
As an observational scientist, I understand that models do not often have the resolution that observers want and that slight
changes in boundary conditions dictated by observations may not make large differences in model results. With this in mind,
I have a few questions that probably need clarification/addressing in the text: Why were the Paxman et al boundary
conditions chosen for this study, rather than the more regionally specific Aitken et al 2016 geomorphologic conditions?
Further, how do the model results presented in this study compare to those of Aitken, which comment on basal velocities
and channel systems visible in subglacial images, but do not prescribe a specific hydrologic system, rather wet and cold-
based regions based on geomorphology?
Past grounding line configurations: The choice of grounding line configurations used in the paleo model runs is not clear.
This may be a place where model resolution is important, but because there is geological data to suggest that the chosen
paleo grounding zone choices are incorrect, the choice of paleo grounding line location warrants further discussion for each
time interval. For instance, is the resolution of the model in this manuscript such that an adjustment of the grounding line out
onto the continental shelf could make a difference to the model output? It might be that the model cannot resolve changes in
the grounding line of 100s of Km, and that is fair and could be mentioned. I think this is what the authors say in the methods
and supplement, but that should be made clear in the main text. Further, if this is the case, how realistic are these model
results, given the complex and relatively fine-scale subglacial topography in the region?
For example, in Aitken’s and other studies, it is clear that the topographic high termed Ridge A might be essential for
stabilizing regional grounding lines—past and present. Given the position of Ridge A at the mouth of the ASB, which means
that there is no reverse sloping bed until ice retreats landward of Ridge A, it might be useful for the authors to both address
this feature and the evidence for ice advance onto the shelf during early ice sheet evolution. Additionally, consideration of
Ridge A is important because (based on the channels in the bedrock on the seaward side of Ridge A; Fernandez et al.,
2018), subglacial meltwater may be really important for getting ice over that high and out onto the shelf.
In the manuscript, it appears that Ridge A is an important constraint on the location of the EO grounding line. Is this a correct
statement? If it is, it should be noted that data from the continental shelf presented by Gulick, Shevenell, et al. (2017; note
that this is the correct citation for this paper) indicate grounded ice expansion onto the shelf, possibly at the EO boundary,
based on existing chronological constraints (not great, but data that exists until the shelf sediments are drilled). This
observation suggests that grounded ice had to make it over Ridge A and onto the shelf as ice in the ASB expanded. The
authors should mention the shelf evidence when discussing their choice of grounding line configuration for the EO
boundary.
The authors should also address how Middle Miocene grounding zone locations were determined especially in light of data
from the continental shelf that indicates at least 10 advances and retreats onto the shelf between what is likely the E-O
boundary and the Late Miocene (Gulick, Shevenell et al., 2017). While the ages of these unconformities are unconstrained,
they are significant in that they also indicate large volumes of meltwater on the shelf based on the presence of tunnel valley
features. It seems that there is an unprecedented opportunity both address apparent data/model disagreement and compare
model results with what we know about subglacial hydrology in the region from the geologic record.
Past sea level: there is substantial data to suggest significant changes in sea level in the past. Was past sea level
considered in the modeling exercise? How might past sea level impact the choice of grounding line locations in the paleo
model runs? We do know that sea level dropped to -30 to -40 m relative to modern day across the EO boundary (Miller et al.,
2020), which likely enabled grounded ice expansion from the ASB across the continental shelf, as observed in the geologic
record. Further, during the Miocene Climate Optimum (~16 Ma), sea levels may have been +50m higher than present (likely
overestimate), while at ~14 Ma, sea levels may have been -40 m lower than present. This is another reason why the authors
really need to clarify if they are talking about the MCO (~16 Ma) or ice expansion and stabilization associated with the
Middle Miocene Climate Transition at ~14 Ma.
Paleo channel locations: there are paleo channel systems identified both in the subglacial landscapes (see Young et al.,
2011, Aitken et al., 2016) inland of Ridge A and on the continental shelf seaward of the current study’s boundaries (see
Gulick, Shevenell et al., 2017; Fernandez et al., 2018; Montelli et al., 2020). How do the model results compare with the
locations of these channels? Some discussion of the modelled channel locations vs observed channel locations would
strengthen the discussion of model results and the impact of the manuscript.
MICI as a viable mass loss mechanism: the authors admit the tenuous nature of the MICI mechanism in ice sheet models.
This reviewer is of the opinion that inclusion of MICI in the runs and in any discussion diminishes the results, as presented
(mostly because the reader is left being skeptical of MICI, rather than thinking about the present modelling study). Would it
be better to think about and address how substantial subglacial meltwater presence might eliminate the need for a MICI-type
mechanism to generate a responsive ice sheet? Such an argument, if possible, would really highlight the need to
understand subglacial hydrologic systems, past and present.
Generally, after reading this manuscript, it seems that the authors have missed an opportunity to compare model runs with
existing observations of subglacial hydrologic systems in this catchment. This is one of the only locations in Antarctica
where such a comparison is possible. Such an exercise would significantly strengthen the believability and impact of the
modeling studies. I recommend such a data-model comparison be undertaken before publication is considered.
A few more minor questions/comments on the manuscript, in no particular order:
This study currently uses outdated CO2 reconstructions. I recommend using the latest CO2 compilation (CENCO2PIP
Consortium, 2023).
Figure 1 and its caption are quite confusing (there might be a typo for the E-O simulation- should it be C and H panels?). It
would be helpful to list the time intervals above the model domains and basal input as in Figure 4, and maybe place vertical
lines between the time intervals.
Why does the Law Dome region disappear in the Mid-Miocene simulation? Is this related to sea level? And, if it is, the same
would be true for the Eocene, would it not?
I don't understand the discussion of ice shelves in past ice configurations. There is no evidence of ice shelf presence in the
Eocene or the middle Miocene, but rather grounded ice on the continental shelves. How does this fact impact the results of
this study?
Fernandez et al (2018) present pretty interesting data for meltwater input to the shelf region during the last deglaciation (see
bedrock channels and stacked grounding zone wedges termed feather moraines in the publication). Would this be a useful
time interval over which to test the model, considering that we have knowledge about the location of the ice sheet and of
subglacial meltwater output/presence during the last deglaciation just based on continental shelf geomorphology.
What happens if surface-derived meltwater is included for the MCO run?

### Reviewer 3

Review of Hayden et al.
This is a very well written paper on changing Aurora subglacial drainage at different climate states that is based on a
finite-element glacier drainage system model which responds to climate forcing through a link between ice thickness and
water pressure at the bed. Using this methodology forced today with BedMachine for the topography and ISMIP6 for the
climate they simulate potential drainage pattern under Totten which seems reasonable.
They then attempt similar situations at the Eocene-Oligocene boundary and at the mid-Miocene. For the latter I think they are
seeking to simulate the Mid-Miocene Climatic Optimum. There are issues with specifically matching the O-18 curve with
CO2 as the authors are undoubtedly aware, but I don’t think this matters for the paper since you are forcing it at two CO2
states roughly equivalent to E-O and MMCO. The specific date does not matter for your study since as noted below, I don’t
think you are yet able to simulate what specifically occurred with the ice sheet and drainage system at the E-O and MMCO.
The larger issues however are three:
1) bed topography has certainly evolved from the Eocene to today and thus what is the sensitivity of the model to this
process since we do not have a E-O or Mid-Mio bedmachine? There are some sentences discussing how it might have
changed but I was left unclear as the expected magnitude and feedbacks if say the deeper basins under ASB we not yet
filled in and we had a subglacier lake scenario, or if the erosion through time has substantially changed the overall gradient
to flatter today than in the E-O run. Can we be confident of these glacial drainage change results in absence of the
topography? Some sensitivity study/discussion is needed to place these results in context on this issue.
2) The ice margin for the ASB portion of East Antarctica is not substantially changing between the E-O, Mid-Mio, Today, and
Future scenarios. There is certainly some retreat and some advance aspects but these are way too small to match the
offshore shelf and slope geophysical data implying presence or absence of grounded ice (Gulick et al., 2017, Nature,
Montelli et al. 2019 GSA Bulletin, McKay et al., 2022, Ant Clim Evol). For instance, at the E-O boundary there were tunnel
valleys > 125 km seaward of the current ice margin which require grounded ice and we have a glacial shelf crossing trough
(Donda et al., 2020, Ant Sci; Hirano et al., 2023, Nature Comm) reaching the shelf edge during the advances. There is strong
data for grounded ice therefore over much of the shelf and within the trough to the shelf edge since there is a large trough
mouth fan for the Totten system active in the Oligocene at least. Therefore your E-O simulation ice margin should be
substantially more advanced to match this geologic evidence. In counterpoint, there appears to have been no evidence of
proximal glacial sedimentary products in the MMCO on the shelf and thus one would infer a much more retreated ice margin
to explain this. Your Mid-Mio simulation is somewhat retreated but probably far too little to explain the absence of glacial
sedimentary facies at the MMCO on the shelf.
3) The lack of greater changes in ice margin at warmer and colder periods imply the current models are missing some key
feedbacks. It could be the effect of ice cliff instability as raised by the authors. However another key change that should
occur is going from colder to warmer based glaciers such as is seen in north versus south Greenland outlet glaciers where
warmer wetter ones moving larger volumes of sediment potentially building glacial moraines or morainal banks, and are
correlated with tunnel valleys existing when advancing onto shelves (e.g., Alaska, North Sea). Colder states act more like
modern Antarctica or the colder based parts of Greenland forming grounding zone wedges instead and substantially less
feedbacks are likely. As Totten system transitioned to this more polar state only the Late Miocene-Pliocene, it is probably
incorrect to assume the subglacial system worked the same way from a more modern polar state as it did in a past more
dynamic state. In other words E-O and Mid-Mio likely dynamically behaved more like the North Sea or Alaska systems than
Pleistocene Antarctica in order to explain the greatly different shelf margin effects and glacial sedimentary products. What
exactly is the change in feedbacks is that allows for much more dynamic advance and retreat cycles is not yet known of
course but some combination of melt water, warm bases, and glacial sediment dynamics are likely involved.
Moving forward with this paper I think the authors need to specifically note how the paleo model runs do not produce
dynamic enough advances to reach the shelf edge during the E-O or leave the shelf entirely ice free during the Mid-Miocene
and then discuss the possible additional feedbacks needed to result in greater ice margin changes. Then discuss what effect
this would have on the subglacial networks that are the focus of this paper. In summary, this paper does a good job with
the paleo models if the bed topography did not differ substantially and if the glacial dynamics did not change going into past
climate states. Issue is we know the ice was a lot further advanced and have evidence of a wetter more dynamic system that
created tunnel valleys, trough mouth fans, and probably intermittent morainal banks … how is this kind of system, one more
representative of the LGM Alaska, North Sea, or West Greenland for instance, differ from what is modeled in this paper?
Given there is clearly a mismatch in ice edge position with the geologic record at least for maximum advance and retreat
climate states, then how can we use this paper’s results to inform us of process without yet being able to include all the
processes required? I think the path forward is to use the paleo model results to discuss how different inputs such as CO2
affect ice thickness and water pressure and drainage without making the argument that this study is faithfully
reproducing the conditions at E-O and Mid-Mio. Consider what you models are not including and how you might then frame your model
results differently since its interesting the tradeoffs observed in water pressure and drainage length in your work, and
considering future scenarios (see below), but these models clearly do not represent the state of the ASB glacial system at
the E-O or mid-Mio.
For the future model runs, I think these are fine and in fact really interesting suggestions for future
states, if the system stays in its current polar mode of dynamics. However, if it switches modes to the way it operated in the
Oligocene to Miocene then there would be expected a much greater dynamic change possibility that could be acknowledged.
On the writing, this paper is remarkably free of typos, has excellently written sentences, and was very clear to read. Only
minor item on that front is that the word further (a concept) is used in two places where the word should be farther (a
distance).
My recommendation is therefore Major Revisions to consider the issues with mismatch to the geologic record and
suggestions of glacial dynamics having a warmer wetter regime with processes not yet included in the finite glacial drainage
system modeling.
Hopefully this review will be helpful and I would be willing to do a re-review as needed,
Sean Gulick

## Round 1 — Authors' Response

Reply to reviewers
The past, present, and future evolution of Aurora Subglacial Basin’s subglacial drainage system
Hayden, Pelle, and Dow
We would like to thank the reviewers for their comments. We have addressed the comments point-
for-point below. The comments are laid out in normal font, and our replies are in italic green font.
Reviewer 1:
This paper uses a subglacial hydrology model to understand how the subglacial drainage system
of the Aurora Subglacial Basin in East Antarctica would respond either in the past or in the future
to changes in ice sheet configuration. A series of warm time periods from the past are tested using
input data from topographic reconstructions or modern topography and from a set of ice sheet
models that have been used to understand warm-period response in this region. The model predicts
where and how much subglacial discharge occurs, how it is routed to the edge of the continent and
thereafter, using a plume model, how that water would translate into melt rates beneath the ice
shelf. The outcomes of each model show quite significant differences in subglacial water flow
pattern and rate, as well as differences in how the water reaches the margin (e.g. through a trunk
vs. multiple outlets) which therefore has a knock-on impact on the pattern of melting under the ice
shelf. A key point is that under retreated ice scenarios, the drainage system tends to become longer
and produces more water, delivering that to the grounding line where it could enhance ice shelf
melting significantly. It is also useful that the authors highlight that its not as simple as using a
paleo warm-period scenario as an analogue for future warming impacts. The work does, as the
authors say, represent the first time the hydraulic system has been investigated for this range of ice
sheet change scenarios and in that respect the key results are impactful. Indeed, it is an interesting
paper and the quality of the work is excellent. The work is largely valid in terms of predicting
subglacial hydraulic changes, but as you can see with my two comments below, there are places
where some additional consideration would help the manuscript. The approach and data are
appropriate, although there are also questions relating to some sensitivity tests (second comment
below).
Suggested Improvements:
However, my first significant concern around the work is that it is not as impactful as it could be
because the points about the impact on ice velocity and buttressing which are used at the end of
the paper to outline why this work is impactful are not actually tested. In other words, outputs of

the impacts on ice behaviour and mass change would be significant, this isn’t directly shown. I
realise you signal that next steps would be to couple things together in an ice sheet model, but
there is a half-way house (via perturbation experiments) which would hammer home the
significance of this work. Thus the impact of the changing hydrologic regime on the ice sheet feels
somewhat speculative at present because the impact on the ice sheet is not fully tested. If it could
be firmed up in some way it would really demonstrate the significance of the results more clearly
as well as becoming of interest to a broader readership.
Thank you for raising this important point and for your help in maximising the impact of our
results. During the time this manuscript was in review, coauthor Pelle and colleagues published
complementary work that presents future 2100 projections of the Aurora Subglacial Basin in a
coupled ice-subglacial hydrology model (ISSM-GlaDS) to test the sensitivity of outlet glacier
behaviour to future subglacial and ocean forcing (Pelle et al., 2024). In their projections, they
found that ice-subglacial water feedbacks (ice shelf melt enhancements and increased grounded
ice basal sliding) increased the ASB sea level contribution by 30%, drove earlier onset of retreat
of Totten’s southern grounding zone by ~25 years, and led to continual accelerated retreat of
Vanderford and Adams Glaciers over the full 83-year projection. These new results confirm our
hypothesis of the strong impact that subglacial processes can have on outlet glacier dynamics.
Thus, in the revised manuscript, we have framed our results in the context of these new findings
(L360-370):
“We note that in a complementary study, Pelle et al.24 developed a coupled ISSM-GlaDS
configuration of ASB and, in projections to 2100, found that subglacial discharge-driven melt
enhancements led to earlier onset of retreat of Totten Glacier’s southern grounding zone by ~25
years and continually accelerated retreat of Vanderford Glacier (up to 10 km of additional retreat
compared to uncoupled “ISSM-only” simulations). That is, while the magnitude of these discharge
melt enhancements is small relative to the background ocean-driven melt signal, their location at
deep grounding line points has cascading impacts on the upstream stress regime of entire glacial
basins. As such, the highly sensitive nature of the melt enhancements presented here highlights the
importance of better constraining subglacial hydrology model inputs and boundary conditions,
which will, in turn, improve simulations of past, present, and future ice sheet dynamics.”
We note that Pelle et al. only ran two subglacial scenarios (a low and high emission climate
forcing) due to the computational cost of running the coupled models through 2100 and thus did
not test the sensitivity of the system to variations in subglacial water input and changes in ice/bed
geometry as we have explored in our manuscript. They also did not perform paleo-simulations.
Nonetheless, we argue that the significance of our work is that we simulate paleo, modern, and
future ASB subglacial hydrology in a consistent modelling framework and can highlight model
sensitivity to the various inputs.

METHODS (L544-564)
“In the Supplementary Material, we include the results of our sensitivity tests (Figs. S22-23 and
Text S1). We focused on basal meltwater production rates, basal velocity, and basal topography.
We run simulations where we set the basal topography to that of BedMachine Antarctica1, but use
the ice surface geometry, basal velocity, and basal melt data from the source publication. Since,
in this test, we are only changing the bed topography but keeping everything else the same as in
the source publication, it allows us to determine the level of control that basal topography has on
the subglacial drainage system. Although the ice surface slope is known to exert a dominant
influence on large-scale subglacial drainage40, water flow paths are also sensitive to basal
topography54–56, with rerouting and water piracy possible under slight variations in bed
topography54–56. Furthermore, large changes in bed slopes over relatively short distances can
cause freeze-on as basal water moves from a region of high to low pressure; this effect has been
incorporated in GlaDS57. Thus, our bed topography test allows us to examine the persistence and
sensitivity of subglacial drainage pathways to bed geometry. Our second sensitivity test imposes
modern-day values for basal topography, basal velocity and basal meltwater production to all
model runs while keeping the ice surface geometry the same as in the source publication. This
allows us to assess the role of ice surface topography on the drainage system evolution. Our final
test examines the role of meltwater production rates by increasing the modern-day initMIP11 basal

could vary for ice sheet geometries governed by different ice sheet model physics.”

We thank the reviewer for raising this point.
Differences in the underlying physics in ice sheet models would likely influence the magnitude and
spatial distribution of basal meltwater production rates. Coupled ice sheet and hydrology
modelling would be required to determine in what direction (increase/decrease) meltwater
production rates would tend in long-term simulations (past and future) and where they would
occur. Since our study aims to capture the overall characteristics of subglacial drainage and ice
shelf basal melt in response to changes in basal conditions and ice geometries, we do not attempt
an intercomparison of modelled subglacial hydrology from the suite of available ice sheet models
(i.e., ISMIP6). However, in the updated submission, we have included an additional sensitivity test
to approximate basal melt variability by taking the modern-day init-MIP basal melt rates and
increasing them everywhere by a factor of 1.5. We believe this gives an approximation of how melt
could vary for ice geometries with different ice sheet physics. The hydrology model outputs under
the 1.5x melt test and those under the standard configuration differ considerably – channel
discharges are up to 3.8x lower in the melt sensitivity test compared to the standard setup. This
result demonstrates the importance of accurately calculating and predicting basal melt rates. We
have added these new results to the supplementary material in Text S1 (L130-167) and Figs S22-
23.
SUPPLEMENTARY MATERIAL
“To further explore the role of basal meltwater production rates, we performed a basal
melt rate sensitivity test in which we increased the modern-day initMIP basal meltwater
production rates everywhere by a factor of 1.5, but used ice geometries, basal topographies, and
basal velocities from the source publication (Fig. S22p-t and Fig. S23p-t). The goal of this test is
to examine how basal melt from models with ice sheet physics that differ from those that informed
our subglacial hydrology modelling experiments (i.e., Li et al.4 and Paxman et al.3) could influence
the subglacial drainage system. Our results from this test indicated that total grounding line
discharge was up to 2.5 and 3.8 times lower than that from the standard simulation for the paleo
and future runs, respectively. These much lower grounding line discharges are likely because,
even after raising the modern melt rate by a factor of 1.5, the meltwater production rates in the
sensitivity test were more than 5.5 times lower than that from the standard Eocene-Oligocene
Boundary 500 ppm No MICI setup and 1.9 times lower in the Mid-Miocene 500 ppm No MICI run.
Compared to the 1.5x melt test (Fig. S22t), the future maximum ice gain run with the standard
setup has higher rates of basal meltwater production across the entire domain, whereas the
sensitivity test shows only isolated points of high basal melt production. There were smaller
differences in channel discharges between the standard setup and the melt sensitivity test for the
maximum ice loss run (Fig. S22s). This may be due to computing limitations that restricted the
simulation time of the maximum ice loss melt sensitivity test to 35,000 days, rather than the 40,000
days used in all other simulations. We also found that the channel lengths were shorter in the 1.5x
melt run and that the location of the dominant channels was also affected. For the Eocene-
Oligocene boundary run, the maximum channel length for this sensitivity test was 122.3 km, ~250
km shorter than that of the standard setup. The maximum channel length for the Mid-Miocene run
was 107.2 km, ~163 km shorter than that of the standard run. Channel lengths were less affected
for the future maximum ice gain run; the longest channel was less than 60 km shorter than in the
standard setup. In the maximum ice loss scenario, the longest channel was ~291 km shorter than
that of the standard run. The spatial distribution of channels was also affected in this sensitivity
test. For both paleo runs, fewer channels crossed the grounding line and the channels that did
develop were less anastomosing. This sensitivity test also resulted in substantial changes to the
extent and distribution of high-pressure regions. For instance, for the Eocene-Oligocene
Boundary, the fraction of the domain at or above 98% of ice overburden pressure was 2.67 times
lower in the sensitivity test, compared to the standard setup. For the Mid-Miocene, only 9.3% of
the domain was at or above 98% of ice overburden pressure, compared to 43.7% in the standard
run. In the sensitivity tests for future runs, the fraction of the domain at high pressure decreased
by a factor of 2.42 and 2.04 for the maximum ice gain and maximum ice loss runs, respectively.
The location of regions at overburden pressure also shifted closer to the grounding line in the
sensitivity runs and did not extend as far inland as in the standard setup. These results underscore
our finding from the modern inputs run, that basal meltwater production rates play a central role
in the development and organisation of the subglacial drainage networks.

Reviewer 2:
I read this well-prepared and clearly written manuscript with great interest because there is
compelling geomorphologic evidence to suggest that subglacial meltwater, either from the
drainage of subglacial lakes or surface melting, may be influencing/may have influenced ice
dynamics in the ASB throughout the Cenozoic. As such, modeling studies are required to assess
the potential impact of subglacial meltwater presence on ice behavior during past warm periods,
particularly in the Totten Glacier catchment, where thinning and ice mass loss and an active
subglacial hydrologic system are presently observed.
Two past time intervals were chosen as part of this study to reflect times when 1) regional ice
volume was larger than at present with higher pCO2 (E-O boundary) and 2) possibly smaller than
present with who knows what pCO2 (Middle Miocene). At least I think this was the goal because
the introduction talks about needing to understand how the subglacial hydrologic system worked
during past warm periods. However, the intervals listed are those of glacial expansion. Climate at
the EO boundary was relatively cold, and if the goal of the middle Miocene study was to hit the
Miocene Climate Optimum, the warmest time interval of the last 30 Ma, that date and ice sheet
configuration should reflect ~16 Ma and not ~14 Ma, when ice expanded and stabilized. The
authors conclude that there have been substantial reorganizations of the subglacial drainage system
over ~40 million years. Well yes, this seems like a pretty safe takeaway for a manuscript.

Miocene. In the manuscript, we have now clarified that, for the Miocene, we are looking at the
Mid-Miocene Climate Transition, as this is what was investigated in the Paxman et al. (2020)
paper from which we acquired the modelled paleo ice geometries. Although, as the reviewer has
mentioned, it would be ideal to model the hydrology during the Miocene Climate Optimum, the
full set of input data (i.e., basal velocity, basal meltwater production rates, ice and bed geometries)
required for our subglacial hydrology model are as of yet unavailable for the Miocene Climate
Optimum. These outputs would need to be generated through paleo ice sheet modelling
experiments, which we do not undertake here. We believe that examining the subglacial hydrology
at the Mid-Miocene Climate Transition is a valuable output from our study since this time period
corresponds to highly variable climate conditions that had considerable impacts on the evolution
of the Antarctic (Gasson et al., 2016; Levy et al., 2016; Shevenell et al., 2008).
There are often mismatches between geomorphological evidence and ice sheet modelling
experiments. Large-scale, long-term ice sheet modelling studies do not include evolving subglacial
hydrology due to the high computational expense, with most ignoring hydrology entirely. Those
few studies that include hydrology only coarsely represent the system. It is conceivable that the
discrepancies between geomorphological features and ice sheet model outputs are due to the lack
of complex hydrological processes in ice sheet models. Our conclusion of the importance of
temporally changing hydrological systems is, therefore, key as it is an area frequently discounted
in ice sheet modelling. In response to this specific comment and to emphasise our goals, in our
revised submission, we have indicated that our simulations are not intended to reproduce the exact
conditions during each time snapshot, but rather to provide a large-scale overview of how the
Aurora Subglacial Basin’s subglacial drainage system is sensitive to changes in ice configurations
and basal (melt, velocity, and topography) conditions, which is a key process for understanding
glacial dynamic drivers in this region (L128-132):
MAIN TEXT:
“The purpose of these experiments is to provide a large-scale overview of how changes in ice
configurations and basal (melt, velocity, and topography) conditions influence Aurora Subglacial

conditions during each of these paleo time snapshots. In the Discussion, we compare our model

As an observational scientist, I understand that models do not often have the resolution that
observers want and that slight changes in boundary conditions dictated by observations may not
make large differences in model results. With this in mind, I have a few questions that probably

Why were the Paxman et al boundary conditions chosen for this study, rather than the more
regionally specific Aitken et al 2016 geomorphologic conditions?
Our study aimed to explore the sensitivity of the subglacial drainage system to changes in ice
geometries that occur due to differences in climate forcing (i.e., different CO2 concentrations and
climate models) as well as highly debated mass loss mechanisms (MICI). To do this, we required
a full suite of inputs for each climate forcing to run the GlaDS hydrology model: basal topography,
basal meltwater production rates, basal velocities, and ice geometries. These data were available
from Paxman et al. (2020) and Li et al. (2023) but not from the Aitken et al. (2016) paper.
Further, how do the model results presented in this study compare to those of Aitken, which
comment on basal velocities and channel systems visible in subglacial images, but do not prescribe
a specific hydrologic system, rather wet and cold-based regions based on geomorphology?
The reviewer raises an excellent point about comparing modelling results to observations, and
thus, we have now added such a comparison in the discussion (L414-451) and in the
supplementary material (L181-212):
MAIN TEXT (L414-451):
“Geomorphological evidence indicates that the ASB experienced several advance and
retreat cycles over the last 34 million years12,19–21,42,43. It has been suggested that surface

Paxman et al.26 was added directly to the bed without seasonal variability. Channel discharge
volumes in this test increased, but the channel locations did not change since surface melt was
concentrated near the grounding line, where channels had already formed. If, in the coming
centuries, surface meltwater was to access the subglacial drainage network, a more dynamic
system reminiscent of the paleo ASB and West Greenland may form, triggering highly variable
grounding line positions and ice flow patterns, even in the absence of MICI. We motivate future
work to build on what we have shown here by investigating variability in surface meltwater inputs
to the bed, as this would provide insights into the stability of the ASB drainage network in the face

Large-scale, long-term ice sheet modelling exercises are often run at coarse resolutions
and with simplified ice dynamics to make the simulations computationally feasible. As a result,
processes such as subglacial hydrology that are known to influence ice dynamics are generally
neglected. The grounding line positions inferred by geomorphological records show larger
variations than those indicated by the ice sheet geometries that were produced by Paxman et al.26
and, therefore, input to our GlaDS simulations. For instance, at the Eocene-Oligocene Boundary,

“In glaciated and formerly glaciated regions, subglacial meltwater has left signatures in

Past sea level: there is substantial data to suggest significant changes in sea level in the past. Was

grounding line locations in the paleo model runs? We do know that sea level dropped to -30 to -

grounded ice expansion from the ASB across the continental shelf, as observed in the geologic
record. Further, during the Miocene Climate Optimum (~16 Ma), sea levels may have been +50m
higher than present (likely overestimate), while at ~14 Ma, sea levels may have been -40 m lower
than present. This is another reason why the authors really need to clarify if they are talking about
the MCO (~16 Ma) or ice expansion and stabilization associated with the Middle Miocene Climate
Transition at ~14 Ma.

of our study. We have also endeavoured to clarify in the main text that we are modelling the

Miocene Climate Transition (14 Mya; hereafter Mid-Miocene) as these intervals correspond to
ice volumes in ASB that are larger and smaller, respectively, than those in the present day26.”

We were intrigued by this suggestion, and thus, we have investigated the distribution of surface
meltwater during the Mid-Miocene run. We ran a Mid-Miocene simulation where the surface
