Reviewer 3:
This is a very well written paper on changing Aurora subglacial basin drainage at different climate
states that is based on a finite-element glacier drainage system model which responds to climate
forcing through a link between ice thickness and water pressure at the bed. Using this methodology
forced today with BedMachine for the topography and ISMIP6 for the climate they simulate
potential drainage pattern under Totten which seems reasonable.
They then attempt similar situations at the Eocene-Oligocene boundary and at the mid-Miocene.
For the latter I think they are seeking to simulate the Mid-Miocene Climatic Optimum. There are
issues with specifically matching the O-18 curve with CO2 as the authors are undoubtedly aware,
but I don’t think this matters for the paper since you are forcing it at two CO2 states roughly
equivalent to E-O and MMCO. The specific date does not matter for your study since as noted
below, I don’t think you are yet able to simulate what specifically occurred with the ice sheet and
drainage system at the E-O and MMCO. The larger issues however are three:
1) bed topography has certainly evolved from the Eocene to today and thus what is the sensitivity
of the model to this process since we do not have a E-O or Mid-Mio bedmachine? There are some
sentences discussing how it might have changed but I was left unclear as the expected magnitude
and feedbacks if say the deeper basins under ASB we not yet filled in and we had a subglacier
lake scenario, or if the erosion through time has substantially changed the overall gradient to flatter
today than in the E-O run. Can we be confident of these glacial drainage change results in absence
of the topography? Some sensitivity study/discussion is needed to place these results in context on
this issue.
We thank the reviewer for raising these points about the bed topography. We realise we could have
been clearer about the sensitivity tests that we performed; Reviewer 1 also mentioned this (please
see our response to their comment above), and in the revised version of the manuscript, we have
now summarised the key findings from Text S1, which details the results of our sensitivity tests.
Below, we provide a review of these sensitivity tests.
Our first test investigated the sensitivity of drainage pathways to bed topography by keeping the
ice surface the same as in the source publication, but varying the bed topography, using either the
time-snapshot-specific bed topography or the modern BedMachine topography. For the paleo
simulations with the BedMachine basal topography, we found that channel lengths were affected,
but the main channel outlet locations remained the same.
In our second test, we kept the ice surface geometry the same as in the source publication but
varied the bed topography (using BedMachine), and modern-day basal velocities and meltwater
production rates (the “modern inputs” sensitivity test). The outputs from this test allowed us to
isolate the role of ice surface geometry in steering water flow. For the Eocene-Oligocene
Boundary, this test indicated that channelised drainage beneath Totten remains dominant,
highlighting the steep surface slopes during this time period. In contrast, drainage through Totten
is lower during the Mid-Miocene, which we attribute to weaker surface slopes. Despite the similar
drainage pathways to the runs with the time-snapshot specific data, the discharge volumes in the
modern inputs sensitivity test were lower than in the runs using time-snapshot-specific data.
Our final sensitivity test, which is a new addition to our manuscript based on comments from
Reviewer 1, investigated the role of variability in basal meltwater production rates. In this test, we
increased the modern basal meltwater production rate everywhere by a factor of 1.5, and applied
it to our paleo and future simulations while keeping the bed and ice geometries, as well as the
basal velocities, the same as those in the source publication. This test approximates the variability
in meltwater production that may result from ice sheet models whose physics differ from those in
the ice sheet models of Paxman et al. (2020) and Li et al. (2023). This test resulted in shorter and
less extensive channels with lower discharges than that of the standard setup, as well as a
reduction in the extent of high pressure regions. Overall, this test highlights the role that basal
meltwater production can have in subglacial drainage development and that tighter constraints
on this basal boundary condition are required.
Regarding the magnitude and feedbacks of bed topography changes, our subglacial hydrology
model is not coupled to erosion and solid earth models, as this is outside the scope of our work.
We are, therefore, unable to provide an estimate of the direction and magnitude of feedbacks
between solid earth uplift, erosional processes, and subglacial hydrology. However, we have
mentioned this limitation in the revised manuscript (L431-451) and in Text S3 of the supplementary
material (see responses to the above comments from Reviewer 2). We note, however, that the input
data from Paxman et al. (2020) did account for isostatic adjustment, erosion, sedimentation,
volcanism, and plate motions in their simulations.
2) The ice margin for the ASB portion of East Antarctica is not substantially changing between
the E-O, Mid-Mio, Today, and Future scenarios. There is certainly some retreat and some advance
aspects but these are way too small to match the offshore shelf and slope geophysical data implying
presence or absence of grounded ice (Gulick et al., 2017, Nature, Montelli et al. 2019 GSA
Bulletin, McKay et al., 2022, Ant Clim Evol). For instance, at the E-O boundary there were tunnel
valleys > 125 km seaward of the current ice margin which require grounded ice and we have a
glacial shelf crossing trough (Donda et al., 2020, Ant Sci; Hirano et al., 2023, Nature Comm)
reaching the shelf edge during the advances. There is strong data for grounded ice therefore over
much of the shelf and within the trough to the shelf edge since there is a large trough mouth fan
for the Totten system active in the Oligocene at least. Therefore your E-O simulation ice margin
should be substantially more advanced to match this geologic evidence. In counterpoint, there
appears to have been no evidence of proximal glacial sedimentary products in the MMCO on the
shelf and thus one would infer a much more retreated ice margin to explain this. Your Mid-Mio
simulation is somewhat retreated but probably far too little to explain the absence of glacial
sedimentary facies at the MMCO on the shelf.
We thank the reviewer for this comment. Reviewer 2 raised similar concerns, which we have
addressed above. Since we are not performing ice sheet modelling experiments, and our subglacial
hydrology model is supplied with data from Paxman et al. (2020), we are unable to change the
location of the grounding line. However, in the revised manuscript we have endeavoured to clarify
that the subglacial drainage systems we model are not intended to be “true” representations of
what the hydrology system looked like in the past but rather to provide a large-scale overview of
how changes in ice configurations and basal conditions influence Aurora Subglacial Basin’s
subglacial drainage system (L128-131):
“The purpose of these experiments is to provide a large-scale overview of how changes in ice
configurations and basal (melt, velocity, and topography) conditions influence Aurora Subglacial
Basin’s subglacial drainage system and are not intended to be interpreted as the exact subglacial
conditions during each of these paleo time snapshots.”
We have also commented on the role that coupled subglacial hydrology and ice dynamics
modelling may have in reproducing paleo grounding line positions (see L434-451 and the
responses to Reviewer 2’s comments above). We hope our findings will inspire such coupled
experiments to better represent ice extent during these time periods.
3) The lack of greater changes in ice margin at warmer and colder periods imply the current models
are missing some key feedbacks. It could be the effect of ice cliff instability as raised by the
authors. However another key change that should occur is going from colder to warmer based
glaciers such as is seen in north versus south Greenland outlet glaciers where warmer wetter ones
moving larger volumes of sediment potentially building glacial moraines or morainal banks, and are
correlated with tunnel valleys existing when advancing onto shelves (e.g., Alaska, North Sea).
Colder states act more like modern Antarctica or the colder based parts of Greenland forming
grounding zone wedges instead and substantially less feedbacks are likely. As Totten system
transitioned to this more polar state only the Late Miocene-Pliocene, it is probably incorrect to
assume the subglacial system worked the same way from a more modern polar state as it did in a
past more dynamic state. In other words E-O and Mid-Mio likely dynamically behaved more like
the North Sea or Alaska systems than Pleistocene Antarctica in order to explain the greatly
different shelf margin effects and glacial sedimentary products. What exactly is the change in
feedbacks is that allows for much more dynamic advance and retreat cycles is not yet known of
course but some combination of melt water, warm bases, and glacial sediment dynamics are likely
involved.
Moving forward with this paper I think the authors need to specifically note how the paleo model
runs do not produce dynamic enough advances to reach the shelf edge during the E-O or leave the
shelf entirely ice free during the Mid-Miocene and then discuss the possible additional feedbacks
needed to result in greater ice margin changes. Then discuss what effect this would have on the
subglacial networks that are the focus of this paper. In summary, this paper does a good job with
the paleo models if the bed topography did not differ substantially and if the glacial dynamics did
not change going into past climate states. Issue is we know the ice was a lot further advanced and
have evidence of a wetter more dynamic system that created tunnel valleys, trough mouth fans,
and probably intermittent morainal banks … how is this kind of system, one more representative
of the LGM Alaska, North Sea, or West Greenland for instance, differ from what is modeled in
this paper? Given there is clearly a mismatch in ice edge position with the geologic record at least
for maximum advance and retreat climate states, then how can we use this paper’s results to inform
us of process without yet being able to include all the processes required? I think the path forward
is to use the paleo model results to discuss how different inputs such as CO2 affect ice thickness
and water pressure and drainage without making the argument that this study is faithfully
reproducing the conditions at E-O and Mid-Mio. Consider what you models are not including and
how you might then frame your model results differently since its interesting the tradeoffs
observed in water pressure and drainage length in your work, and considering future scenarios (see
below), but these models clearly do not represent the state of the ASB glacial system at the E-O or
mid-Mio.
We thank the reviewer for raising these points. We’d like to emphasise that our work is exploratory
in nature, being the first to compare past, present, and future hydrology and ice shelf melt using
evolving 2-D models. Therefore, we are not attempting to recreate the exact conditions at each
time snapshot. We do, however, agree that acknowledging the limitations of our modelling
approach is important for framing the results and their implications, and reviewer 2 raised similar
concerns about our modelled system and that suggested by the paleo record. In the discussion of
our revised manuscript and in Text S3, we have noted the discrepancies between our modelling
results and observations. We have now provided suggestions for future work such that a closer
match between model outputs and geomorphological evidence can be obtained. We have
addressed the role of solid earth uplift, surface meltwater and erosion processes in the region and
motivated the use of coupled ice sheet-hydrology models as this may lead to grounding line
locations more representative of those documented in the paleo record. We hope these
amendments, along with our clarification of the aim and intention of this manuscript, have satisfied
these concerns.
For the future model runs, I think these are fine and in fact really interesting suggestions for future
states, if the system stays in its current polar mode of dynamics. However, if it switches modes to
the way it operated in the Oligocene to Miocene then there would be expected a much greater
dynamic change possibility that could be acknowledged.
We thank the reviewer for the positive feedback, and we have now made this comparison in the
revised version (L424-427):
“If, in the coming centuries, surface meltwater were to access the subglacial drainage network,
a more dynamic system reminiscent of the paleo ASB and West Greenland may form, triggering
highly variable grounding line positions and ice flow patterns, even in the absence of MICI.”
On the writing, this paper is remarkably free of typos, has excellently written sentences, and was
very clear to read. Only minor item on that front is that the word further (a concept) is used in two
places where the word should be farther (a distance).
We have made this correction.
My recommendation is therefore Major Revisions to consider the issues with mismatch to the
geologic record and suggestions of glacial dynamics having a warmer wetter regime with processes
not yet included in the finite glacial drainage system modeling.
Hopefully this review will be helpful and I would be willing to do a re-review as needed,
Sean Gulick

Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):
This is a revised submission of a very interesting and well written modeling study by Hayden et al
on the effects of subglacial hydrology on ice sheet dynamics in the Aurora subglacial basin, East
Antarctica. In general, I accept a lot of the response to reviewers aspects that the authors raised
and appreciate the edited discussion in the main text and supplemental.
Thank you.
However, I recommend an additional minor set of edits which are a suggestion to be more specific
in the caveats starting with line 430. Right now the paper lumps the geological evidence under the
terminology "geomorphologic evidence" (or some variant) which is partly correct but misses also
the glacial sequence stratigraphy on the shelf (i.e. the geologic record) published in several of the
papers you cite in this section.
We agree that expanding the discussion to include a more detailed comparison between the
stratigraphic record and our results would strengthen the manuscript. In the revised manuscript
and summarised below, we address the reviewer’s suggestions.
So I strongly recommend not just mentioning that the modeling of ice extents is known to be
inconsistent with shelf morphology (e.g. presence of a shelf crossing trough and lateral moraines)
during ice advances, but also note that it is inconsistent with presence of stratigraphic indicators
of grounded ice (e.g. tunnel valleys and sedimentary deposits) both for the advanced and retreated
positions of the ASB marine terminating ice.
We thank the reviewer for pointing this out. In the revised manuscript, we have explicitly stated
the geologic markers in the sedimentary record and how our domains and model results compare
to this evidence.
L434-440: “In the sediment stratigraphy of the ASB’s continental margin, there are repeat
signatures of sediment wedges and bedrock channels shaped by subglacial meltwater flows20,21,43,
dating from the Eocene to the Miocene. These features are located beyond the grounding lines of
the Paxman et al.26 data (and, hence, our GlaDS domains) and indicate that fluctuations in ASB
terminus positions were much larger during both cold and warm climate states than what Paxman
et al.’s26 results suggest. These mismatches in grounding line locations, in turn, affect our ability
to compare our modelled hydrologic pathways to those preserved in the geologic record.”
I understand ice extents are baked into the boundary conditions of your model so you cannot
change this aspect, but you can make it clear that your modeling therefore greatly under-predicts
the terminus response due warm states (e.g. the MMCO) and cold states (e.g. E/O boundary)
We have endeavoured to clarify this in the response to the preceding comment.
and a more complete list of the key factors/feedbacks could matter and need to be integrated into
future studies. For instance I recommend adding in that one key feedback not included within this
modeling or in Paxman et al is the role of subglacial sediments in addition to subglacial hydrology.
For instance your long hydrologic conduits very likely should become tunnel valleys in the model
with a feedback built in that these are erosive sub glacially but depositional near the terminus and
thus can provide a direct feedback to the ground line stability, which likely then changes under
different flow regimes/with connection to surface melt/with different hydrologic pressures (as you
note).
We agree that expanding our discussion of the feedback mechanisms at play but not currently
included in our or Paxman et al.’s modelling approaches is important for highlighting future
research priorities. The revised manuscript describes the interactions between erosional and
depositional processes, subglacial hydrology, and ice dynamics.
L444-458: “The absence of subglacial hydrology in Paxman et al.’s26 model could have also
affected their computed rates and patterns of subglacial erosion and sediment deposition, with
cascading effects on the locations and advance/retreat rates of terminus positions. For example,
subglacial meltwater that is continuously routed along the same path could create the above-
mentioned bedrock channels under grounded ice. The sediment mobilised by subglacial meltwater
could then be deposited further offshore, where it could lead to the formation of topographic
pinning points that stabilise grounding line positions and affect ice dynamics. Whereas Paxman et

depositional processes, and therefore, we are unable to capture the redistribution of sediment in
the system by subglacial meltwater and the resulting geomorphological features. The limitations

erosion, sedimentation, and hydrology in ice sheet models since the bed is not static but instead

I don't think you can ignore the role of erosion/redistribution of sediment within the subglacial
